questions.prompt: Based on the cases discussed in Allarey v. Dela Cruz, in which situation was res ipsa loquitur applied to hold a physician liable?

choices.A: A mother who died of placenta accreta, a complication arising from the pregnancy itself.
choices.B: A patient whose actual cause of injury had already been identified and established.
choices.C: A mother who, after delivering a baby, was found with a gaping wound on her arm, an injury that could not have happened unless negligence had set in somewhere.
choices.D: A patient whose death required expert opinion to connect it to the treatment.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court cited Cantre v. Spouses Go, where res ipsa loquitur was applied because a gaping wound on the patient's arm is not an ordinary occurrence in delivering a baby, and such "injury could not have happened unless negligence had set in somewhere." **A is wrong:** that is Allarey itself, where the doctrine was held inapplicable. **B is wrong:** Borromeo holds the doctrine does not apply where the actual cause had been identified or established. **D is wrong:** where expert opinion is needed to link the injury to the treatment, the doctrine, which rests on common knowledge, does not fit. **Bar trap:** the doctrine fits injuries a layman can judge, not complications that need a specialist to explain.

source.caseTitle: Allarey, et al. v. Dela Cruz and Manila East Medical Center, Inc.
source.part: Ruling of the Court, The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur cannot be applied (citing Cantre and Borromeo)
source.excerpt: A review of medical negligence cases brought to this Court reveals that the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur is applied only to exceptional circumstances where the failure to observe due care which caused injury to the patient is readily apparent to a layman and is within the exclusive control of the erring physician. In Cantre v. Spouses Go, the Court applied the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur to justify declaring the physician liable. The Court explained that the gaping wound on the patient's arm is not an ordinary occurrence in the act of delivering a baby and that such "injury could not have happened unless negligence had set in somewhere." In Borromeo v. Family Care Hospital, Inc., the Court explained that the application of the doctrine "require[s] expert opinion to establish the culpability of the defendant doctor." It also does not apply to cases where the actual cause of the injury had been identified or established.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: What is medical malpractice or medical negligence? What must a patient prove, and what evidence is required in a case against an anesthesiologist for a patient's death under anesthesia? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Medical malpractice, more appropriately medical negligence, is the type of claim available to a victim to redress a wrong committed by a medical professional which has caused bodily harm. The patient must prove duty, breach, injury and proximate causation. Against an anesthesiologist, the proof is two-pronged: the recognized standards of the medical community in that kind of case, and the physician's negligent departure from that standard.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Garcia-Rueda v. Pascasio, the Court held that the patient must prove that the health care provider failed to do what a reasonably prudent provider would have done, or did what a reasonably prudent provider would not have done, and that this caused injury. By accepting a case, the doctors represent that they have the training and skill of physicians in the same field and will use them; they must use at least the level of care of any reasonably competent doctor under the same circumstances, and a breach of these duties that injures the patient constitutes actionable malpractice. In anesthesia cases, expert testimony and res ipsa loquitur have both been applied, and two-pronged evidence is essentially required.
suggestedAnswer.application: A widow suing over her husband's death after anesthesia must show the physician-patient relationship (created when the doctors accepted the case), the recognized standard for administering anesthesia in that kind of operation, the anesthesiologist's negligent departure from it, the death, and that the departure caused the death.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Medical negligence is proved through duty, breach, injury and proximate causation; in anesthesia cases, through the standard of the medical community and the departure from it. **Bar trap:** the standard is set by the medical community in the particular kind of case, not by the court's or the family's own idea of what should have been done.

keyPoints: Definition: the claim to redress a wrong by a medical professional that caused bodily harm
Elements: duty, breach, injury, proximate causation
Duty arises from the physician-patient relationship created by accepting the case
Anesthesia cases: two-pronged evidence, the recognized standard of the medical community and the negligent departure from it

source.caseTitle: Garcia-Rueda v. Pascasio, et al.
source.part: A word on medical malpractice or negligence cases
source.excerpt: In its simplest terms, the type of lawsuit which has been called medical malpractice or, more appropriately, medical negligence, is that type of claim which a victim has available to him or her to redress a wrong committed by a medical professional which has caused bodily harm. In order to successfully pursue such a claim, a patient must prove that a health care provider, in most cases a physician, either failed to do something which a reasonably prudent health care provider would have done, or that he or she did something that a reasonably prudent provider would not have done; and that that failure or action caused injury to the patient. Hence, there are four elements involved in medical negligence cases: duty, breach, injury and proximate causation. Evidently, when the victim employed the services of Dr. Antonio and Dr. Reyes, a physician-patient relationship was created. In accepting the case, Dr. Antonio and Dr. Reyes in effect represented that, having the needed training and skill possessed by physicians and surgeons practicing in the same field, they will employ such training, care and skill in the treatment of their patients. They have a duty to use at least the same level of care that any other reasonably competent doctor would use to treat a condition under the same circumstances. The breach of these professional duties of skill and care, or their improper performance, by a physician surgeon whereby the patient is injured in body or in health, constitutes actionable malpractice. … Moreover, in malpractice or negligence cases involving the administration of anaesthesia, the necessity of expert testimony and the availability of the charge of res ipsa loquitur to the plaintiff; have been applied in actions against anaesthesiologists to hold the defendant liable for the death or injury of a patient under excessive or improper anaesthesia. Essentially, it requires two-pronged evidence: evidence as to the recognized standards of the medical community in the particular kind of case, and a showing that the physician in question negligently departed from this standard in his treatment.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A patient died a few hours after surgery. The NBI found that the anesthesiologist did not interview the patient before the operation, that the death could have been averted had the proper drug been given for the symptoms of malignant hyperthermia, and that an antidote was readily available. The prosecutor dismissed the homicide-through-reckless-imprudence complaint, saying the cause of death was uncertain and the doctors' competence could not be judged at that stage. Discuss causation as an element of medical negligence, and state whether the dismissal was proper.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Causation is divided into two inquiries: whether the doctor's actions in fact caused the harm, and whether they were the proximate cause of the injury. On these facts the allegation of negligence was not baseless, and the technical questions of competence and causation were better resolved at a full trial, so a dismissal at the preliminary investigation was not proper.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Garcia-Rueda v. Pascasio, the Court held that a causal connection was discernible from the death following the anesthesiologist's alleged negligence, which, if confirmed, warranted the filing of the criminal case. It noted the NBI findings that no pre-operation interview was done, that death could have been averted with the proper drug for malignant hyperthermia, and that an antidote was available. Want of competence or diligence is evidentiary and best passed upon after a full-blown trial, since it is virtually impossible to judge a medical negligence case without extensive investigation and consultation with experts; prosecutors are not in a competent position to pass judgment on such technical matters, especially with conflicting findings. A preliminary investigation only determines probable cause, which does not require evidence sufficient for conviction.
suggestedAnswer.application: The NBI's findings give a reasonable ground to believe that the anesthesiologist's omissions in fact caused, and were the proximate cause of, the death. Uncertainty about the precise cause is a matter for trial, not a ground to dismiss at the probable-cause stage. Why the precautionary measures were disregarded must be explained, and the place for that is the trial.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Causation has two parts, cause in fact and proximate cause; the NBI findings made out probable cause, so the complaint should have proceeded to trial. **Bar trap:** a preliminary investigation does not decide guilt; doubts about technical medical issues favor ventilating them at trial.

keyPoints: Causation has two inquiries: cause in fact, and proximate cause
A causal connection was discernible from death following the alleged negligent administration of anesthesia
Want of competence or diligence is evidentiary and best decided after a full trial with expert evidence
Probable cause does not require evidence sufficient to convict

source.caseTitle: Garcia-Rueda v. Pascasio, et al.
source.part: A word on medical malpractice or negligence cases (causation)
source.excerpt: In the instant case, no less than the NBI pronounced after conducting an autopsy that there was indeed negligence on the part of the attending physicians in administering the anaesthesia. The fact of want of competence or diligence is evidentiary in nature, the veracity of which can best be passed upon after a full-blown trial for it is virtually impossible to ascertain the merits of a medical negligence case without extensive investigation, research, evaluation and consultations with medical experts. Clearly, the City Prosecutors are not in a competent position to pass judgment on such a technical matter, especially when there are conflicting evidence and findings. The bases of a party's accusation and defenses are better ventilated at the trial proper than at the preliminary investigation. … Another element in medical negligence cases is causation which is divided into two inquiries: whether the doctor's actions in fact caused the harm to the patient and whether these were the proximate cause of the patient's injury. Indeed here, a causal connection is discernible from the occurrence of the victim's death after the negligent act of the anaesthesiologist in administering the anesthesia, a fact which, if confirmed, should warrant the filing of the appropriate criminal case. To be sure, the allegation of negligence is not entirely baseless. Moreover, the NBI deduced that the attending surgeons did not conduct the necessary interview of the patient prior to the operation. It appears that the cause of the death of the victim could have been averted had the proper drug been applied to cope with the symptoms of malignant hyperthermia. Also, we cannot ignore the fact that an antidote was readily available to counteract whatever deleterious effect the anaesthesia might produce. Why these precautionary measures were disregarded must be sufficiently explained.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: After her complaint for homicide through reckless imprudence against her late husband's doctors was passed among several city prosecutors and finally dismissed as to the anesthesiologist, Lorna charged the prosecutors before the Ombudsman with violating Section 3(e) of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act for manifest partiality. The Ombudsman dismissed her complaint for lack of evidence. On certiorari, will the Supreme Court set aside the Ombudsman's action? What was Lorna's better remedy?

suggestedAnswer.answer: No, unless the Ombudsman gravely abused its discretion, which is not shown by a dismissal for lack of evidence. Lorna's better and more logical remedy was to appeal the prosecutors' resolution dismissing her criminal complaint to the Secretary of Justice.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Garcia-Rueda v. Pascasio, the Court held that courts will not interfere with the Ombudsman's discretion to determine whether a criminal case should be filed, except when there is grave abuse of discretion, defined as a power exercised in an arbitrary or despotic manner by reason of passion or personal hostility so patent and gross as to amount to an evasion of positive duty. It found the widow's choice of a graft charge surprising, and held that the better remedy was an appeal to the Secretary of Justice under the DOJ rules on appeals from resolutions in preliminary investigations, which allow appeal from a resolution dismissing a criminal complaint; the Secretary may reverse, affirm or modify it.
suggestedAnswer.application: The Ombudsman acted within its power in dismissing the graft complaint, though it should have inquired into the unexplained transfers among prosecutors. The prosecutors' resolution dismissing the complaint against the anesthesiologist was precisely the kind of resolution appealable to the Secretary of Justice. So the Court dismissed the petition without prejudice to that appeal.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The petition fails; Lorna should appeal the dismissal to the Secretary of Justice. **Bar trap:** a grievance against how prosecutors handled a medical-negligence complaint is not, by itself, a graft case; use the remedy aimed at the dismissal itself.

keyPoints: Courts do not interfere with the Ombudsman's discretion absent grave abuse of discretion
Grave abuse: arbitrary or despotic exercise of power, so patent and gross as to amount to evasion of a positive duty
The better remedy: appeal the prosecutor's dismissal to the Secretary of Justice, who may reverse, affirm or modify it
The petition was dismissed without prejudice to that appeal

source.caseTitle: Garcia-Rueda v. Pascasio, et al.
source.part: Ruling, the remedy against the dismissal of a criminal complaint
source.excerpt: While the Ombudsman has the full discretion to determine whether or not a criminal case should be filed, this Court is not precluded from reviewing the Ombudsman's action when there is an abuse of discretion, in which case Rule 65 of the Rules of Court may exceptionally be invoked pursuant to Section I, Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution. In this regard, "grave abuse of discretion" has been defined as "where a power is exercised in an arbitrary or despotic manner by reason of passion or personal hostility so patent and gross as to amount to evasion of positive duty or virtual refusal to perform a duty enjoined by, or in contemplation of law. … To our mind, the better and more logical remedy under the circumstances would have been to appeal the resolution of the City Prosecutors dismissing the criminal complaint to the Secretary of Justice under the Department of Justice's Order No. 223, otherwise known as the "1993 Revised Rules on Appeals From Resolutions In Preliminary Investigations/Reinvestigations," as amended by Department Order No. 359, Section 1 of which provides: … In exercising his discretion under the circumstances, the Ombudsman acted within his power and authority in dismissing the complaint against the Prosecutors and this Court will not interfere with the same.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Mila, healthy and neurologically sound, was scheduled for a routine gallbladder operation. While she was under anesthesia, and before any incision was made, she suffered brain damage and fell into a coma. Her family sues the surgeon and the anesthesiologist and invokes res ipsa loquitur. The doctors answer that the doctrine cannot apply in malpractice suits, which always require expert testimony. Is the defense correct? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Res ipsa loquitur applies: a sound, unaffected part of Mila's body (her brain) was injured while she was unconscious and under the exclusive control of the doctors, and such an injury does not normally occur in a gallbladder operation without negligence.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Ramos v. Court of Appeals (1999), the Court held that medical malpractice cases do not escape the doctrine. Although expert testimony is generally relied upon in malpractice suits, when res ipsa loquitur applies the need for it is dispensed with because the injury itself provides the proof of negligence. The doctrine does not apply to the merits of a diagnosis or a scientific treatment, or where the only showing is that the desired result was not accomplished; the real question is whether an extraordinary incident or unusual event outside the routine performance occurred that would reasonably speak to the average man as the negligent cause.
suggestedAnswer.application: Mila delivered herself to the care, custody and control of the doctors, who had exclusive control of the anesthesia and the endotracheal tube. She could not have contributed, being unconscious. A person put under anesthesia is not normally rendered decerebrate if the proper procedure is followed, and her claim does not rest on a failed operation or a wrong diagnosis, since no operation was ever performed.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The defense is wrong; the doctrine applies and the doctors must explain. **Bar trap:** the Court also warned that the doctrine does not apply to any and all anesthesia cases; each case must be viewed in its own light.

keyPoints: Malpractice cases do not escape res ipsa loquitur; when it applies, expert testimony is dispensed with
A sound part of the body was injured while the patient was unconscious and under the doctors' exclusive control
Brain damage does not normally occur in a routine gallbladder operation without negligence
Not a case of failure to secure results or a wrong diagnosis; no operation was performed
The doctrine does not apply to all anesthesia cases; each is judged on its facts

source.caseTitle: Ramos, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Ruling, the application of res ipsa loquitur
source.excerpt: Medical malpractice cases do not escape the application of this doctrine. … Although generally, expert medical testimony is relied upon in malpractice suits to prove that a physician has done a negligent act or that he has deviated from the standard medical procedure, when the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur is availed by the plaintiff, the need for expert medical testimony is dispensed with because the injury itself provides the proof of negligence. … The real question, therefore, is whether or not in the process of the operation any extraordinary incident or unusual event outside of the routine performance occurred which is beyond the regular scope of customary professional activity in such operations, which, if unexplained would themselves reasonably speak to the average man as the negligent cause or causes of the untoward consequence. … Considering that a sound and unaffected member of the body (the brain) is injured or destroyed while the patient is unconscious and under the immediate and exclusive control of the physicians, we hold that a practical administration of justice dictates the application of res ipsa loquitur. Upon these facts and under these circumstances the Court would be able to say, as a matter of common knowledge and observation, if negligence attended the management and care of the patient. Moreover, the liability of the physicians and the hospital in this case is not predicated upon an alleged failure to secure the desired results of an operation nor on an alleged lack of skill in the diagnosis or treatment as in fact no operation or treatment was ever performed on Erlinda. … Nonetheless, in holding that res ipsa loquitur is available to the present case we are not saying that the doctrine is applicable in any and all cases where injury occurs to a patient while under anesthesia, or to any and all anesthesia cases. Each case must be viewed in its own light and scrutinized in order to be within the res ipsa loquitur coverage.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: An anesthesiologist met her patient for the first time in the operating room, an hour before an elective operation, and had great difficulty inserting the breathing tube; the patient suffered brain damage from lack of oxygen. She explains that she usually skips the pre-operative visit in elective cases with normal clearances, and that the patient's short neck and protruding teeth made the intubation hard. Was she negligent, and was her negligence the proximate cause of the injury? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes to both. Failing to do a pre-operative evaluation before an elective operation was negligence, and the resulting faulty intubation was the proximate cause of the brain damage.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Ramos v. Court of Appeals (1999), the Court held that pre-operative evaluation before anesthesia is universally observed to lessen anesthetic accidents, and includes a thorough analysis of the patient's airway. In elective procedures, which can wait, the anesthesiologist has the luxury of time for a proper interview and evaluation; it is in emergencies that there is hardly time. Seeing the patient for the first time an hour before an elective operation was "an act of exceptional negligence and professional irresponsibility." Proximate cause is that which, in natural and continuous sequence, unbroken by any efficient intervening cause, produces injury, and without which the result would not have occurred.
suggestedAnswer.application: Her explanation has it backwards: elective cases are exactly where she had time to evaluate. A short neck and protruding teeth are what a pre-operative airway assessment is meant to detect, so that the intubation can be prepared for; raised only after the fact, they are an afterthought. The failed intubation delayed oxygen to the lungs, the patient turned cyanotic, and the brain was deprived of oxygen for four to five minutes: an unbroken chain from the faulty intubation to the injury.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: She was negligent, and her negligence was the proximate cause. **Bar trap:** do not accept "elective, so no pre-operative visit needed"; the Court said the opposite is true.

keyPoints: Pre-operative evaluation, including airway assessment, is universally observed to lessen anesthetic accidents
Elective surgery leaves time for evaluation; emergencies do not
Seeing the patient first an hour before an elective operation was exceptional negligence
Anatomical difficulties are what the evaluation is meant to discover; they are no excuse after the fact
Proximate cause: natural and continuous sequence, unbroken by an efficient intervening cause

source.caseTitle: Ramos, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Ruling, the negligence of the anesthesiologist and proximate cause
source.excerpt: The pre-operative evaluation of a patient prior to the administration of anesthesia is universally observed to lessen the possibility of anesthetic accidents. … In the case at bar, respondent Dra. Gutierrez admitted that she saw Erlinda for the first time on the day of the operation itself, on 17 June 1985. Before this date, no prior consultations with, or pre-operative evaluation of Erlinda was done by her. Until the day of the operation, respondent Dra. Gutierrez was unaware of the physiological make-up and needs of Erlinda. She was likewise not properly informed of the possible difficulties she would face during the administration of anesthesia to Erlinda. Respondent Dra. Gutierrez' act of seeing her patient for the first time only an hour before the scheduled operative procedure was, therefore, an act of exceptional negligence and professional irresponsibility. … However, the exact opposite is true. In an emergency procedure, there is hardly enough time available for the fastidious demands of pre-operative procedure so that an anesthesiologist is able to see the patient only a few minutes before surgery, if at all. Elective procedures, on the other hand, are operative procedures that can wait for days, weeks or even months. Hence, in these cases, the anesthesiologist possesses the luxury of time to be at the patient's beside to do a proper interview and clinical evaluation. … Proximate cause has been defined as that which, in natural and continuous sequence, unbroken by any efficient intervening cause, produces injury, and without which the result would not have occurred.

questions.prompt: Dr. Reyes, a surgeon, promised his patient a good anesthesiologist and chose one. He then scheduled another operation in a different hospital at the same time, and arrived three hours late. When he arrived, the anesthesiologist had difficulty intubating the patient, who suffered brain damage. Dr. Reyes argues that the anesthesia was the anesthesiologist's specialty and responsibility, not his. Is Dr. Reyes liable? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. As the head of the surgical team, the "captain of the ship," Dr. Reyes was responsible for seeing that those under him performed their tasks properly, and he failed in that duty.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Ramos v. Court of Appeals (1999), the Court held that, as the so-called captain of the ship, it is the surgeon's responsibility to see to it that those under him perform their task in the proper manner. Dr. Hosaka's negligence lay in failing to exercise his authority by not determining whether his anesthesiologist observed proper anesthesia protocols, and in scheduling another procedure at the same time and arriving over three hours late, leaving little or no time to confer with the anesthesiologist. He therefore shared equal responsibility.
suggestedAnswer.application: Dr. Reyes chose the anesthesiologist, did nothing to verify that she followed proper protocol, and, by double-booking himself and arriving three hours late, had no time to confer with her about the anesthesia. That the anesthesia was another specialist's task does not relieve the captain of the team of his own duty of supervision.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Dr. Reyes is solidarily liable with the anesthesiologist. **Bar trap:** "it was not my specialty" does not help the lead surgeon. (In the 2002 resolution in the same case, the Court kept the two doctors solidarily liable but absolved the hospital, finding no employer-employee relationship with them.)

keyPoints: The lead surgeon is the captain of the ship
He must see to it that those under him perform their tasks properly
Failure to determine whether the anesthesiologist observed proper protocols
Double-booking and arriving three hours late left no time to confer about the anesthesia
He shares equal responsibility with the anesthesiologist

source.caseTitle: Ramos, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Ruling, the responsibility of Dr. Hosaka as captain of the ship
source.excerpt: We now determine the responsibility of respondent Dr. Orlino Hosaka as the head of the surgical team. As the so-called "captain of the ship," it is the surgeon's responsibility to see to it that those under him perform their task in the proper manner. Respondent Dr. Hosaka's negligence can be found in his failure to exercise the proper authority (as the "captain" of the operative team) in not determining if his anesthesiologist observed proper anesthesia protocols. In fact, no evidence on record exists to show that respondent Dr. Hosaka verified if respondent Dra. Gutierrez properly intubated the patient. Furthermore, it does not escape us that respondent Dr. Hosaka had scheduled another procedure in a different hospital at the same time as Erlinda's cholecystectomy, and was in fact over three hours late for the latter's operation. Because of this, he had little or no time to confer with his anesthesiologist regarding the anesthesia delivery. This indicates that he was remiss in his professional duties towards his patient. Thus, he shares equal responsibility for the events which resulted in Erlinda's condition.

questions.prompt: In Ramos v. Court of Appeals (1999), the Court of Appeals disregarded the testimony of the patient's sister-in-law, a nursing dean, that the anesthesiologist failed to intubate the patient, because nurses do not intubate. How did the Supreme Court rule?

choices.A: It agreed, because only an anesthesiologist may testify on whether an intubation succeeded.
choices.B: It disagreed: although not an anesthesiologist, she could testify on matters she was capable of observing, such as the statements and acts of the physician, external appearances and manifest conditions, which is allowed under res ipsa loquitur.
choices.C: It agreed, because a relative of the patient is presumed biased.
choices.D: It disagreed, because nurses are experts in all hospital procedures.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court held that although she was not an anesthesiologist, the witness "can very well testify upon matters on which she is capable of observing such as, the statements and acts of the physician and surgeon, external appearances, and manifest conditions which are observable by any one," which is precisely allowed under res ipsa loquitur; expert testimony is unnecessary where the lack of care is obvious. It even took judicial notice that anesthesia procedures had become so common that an ordinary person can tell if it was administered properly. **A is wrong:** that was the Court of Appeals' view, which was rejected. **C is wrong:** the Court found her testimony straightforward and credible, and it was corroborated by the anesthesiologist's own admission. **D is wrong:** the Court did not treat her as an expert in all procedures; it relied on what she observed and on her clinical experience. **Bar trap:** a non-expert may testify on what anyone can observe.

source.caseTitle: Ramos, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Ruling, the testimony of Dean Herminda Cruz
source.excerpt: We do not agree with the above reasoning of the appellate court. Although witness Cruz is not an anesthesiologist, she can very well testify upon matters on which she is capable of observing such as, the statements and acts of the physician and surgeon, external appearances, and manifest conditions which are observable by any one. This is precisely allowed under the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur where the testimony of expert witnesses is not required. It is the accepted rule that expert testimony is not necessary for the proof of negligence in non-technical matters or those of which an ordinary person may be expected to have knowledge, or where the lack of skill or want of care is so obvious as to render expert testimony unnecessary. We take judicial notice of the fact that anesthesia procedures have become so common, that even an ordinary person can tell if it was administered properly.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: To prove that a patient's brain damage came from an allergic reaction to the anesthetic drug, the defense in Ramos v. Court of Appeals (1999) presented a pulmonologist. Why did the Court reject his opinion?

choices.A: Because a pulmonologist may never testify in a malpractice case.
choices.B: Because he was related to one of the defendants.
choices.C: Because he testified after the period for presenting evidence had lapsed.
choices.D: Because he was not an anesthesiologist, an allergologist or a pharmacologist, and formed his opinion on the drug only from reading references, not from practical experience.

questions.explanation: **D is correct.** The Court held that the pulmonologist "cannot be considered an authority in the field of anesthesiology simply because he is not an anesthesiologist," was not an allergologist who could give an opinion on allergic processes, and was not a pharmacologist who could explain the drug's effects; he admitted forming his opinions from reading certain references rather than from practical experience with the drug. **A is wrong:** the problem was not his specialty as such but that it did not match the issues. **B and C are wrong:** neither reason appears in the decision. **Bar trap:** an expert must be qualified on the very question in issue (compare Reyes v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital, where a pathologist's opinion on a typhoid diagnosis was rejected).

source.caseTitle: Ramos, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Ruling, the testimony of Dr. Jamora
source.excerpt: First of all, Dr. Jamora cannot be considered an authority in the field of anesthesiology simply because he is not an anesthesiologist. Since Dr. Jamora is a pulmonologist, he could not have been capable of properly enlightening the court about anesthesia practice and procedure and their complications. Dr. Jamora is likewise not an allergologist and could not therefore properly advance expert opinion on allergic-mediated processes. Moreover, he is not a pharmacologist and, as such, could not have been capable, as an expert would, of explaining to the court the pharmacologic and toxic effects of the supposed culprit, Thiopental Sodium (Pentothal). The inappropriateness and absurdity of accepting Dr. Jamora's testimony as an expert witness in the anesthetic practice of Pentothal administration is further supported by his own admission that he formulated his opinions on the drug not from the practical experience gained by a specialist or expert in the administration and use of Sodium Pentothal on patients, but only from reading certain references, to wit:

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: "That which, in natural and continuous sequence, unbroken by any efficient intervening cause, produces injury, and without which the result would not have occurred." As defined in Ramos v. Court of Appeals (1999), this is

choices.A: proximate cause.
choices.B: fortuitous event.
choices.C: contributory negligence.
choices.D: res ipsa loquitur.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court defined proximate cause in these words and added that it is "the dominant, moving or producing cause"; applying it, the faulty intubation was the proximate cause of Erlinda's brain damage. **B is wrong:** a fortuitous event is the opposite of a cause attributable to someone's fault; the decision does not use it. **C is wrong:** contributory negligence is negligence of the injured person; the Court held Erlinda, being unconscious, could not have contributed. **D is wrong:** res ipsa loquitur is a rule of evidence that raises a presumption of negligence. **Bar trap:** the key words are "natural and continuous sequence" and "unbroken by any efficient intervening cause."

source.caseTitle: Ramos, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Ruling, proximate cause
source.excerpt: Proximate cause has been defined as that which, in natural and continuous sequence, unbroken by any efficient intervening cause, produces injury, and without which the result would not have occurred. An injury or damage is proximately caused by an act or a failure to act, whenever it appears from the evidence in the case, that the act or omission played a substantial part in bringing about or actually causing the injury or damage; and that the injury or damage was either a direct result or a reasonably probable consequence of the act or omission. It is the dominant, moving or producing cause.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Ramos v. Court of Appeals (1999), the Court awarded temperate damages on top of actual damages to the family of a patient left comatose. What was its reason?

choices.A: Temperate damages are always awarded whenever moral damages are awarded.
choices.B: Temperate damages replace actual damages whenever receipts are incomplete.
choices.C: Where the injury is chronic and continuing, temperate damages may be awarded on top of actual damages to meet pecuniary loss certain to be suffered but which cannot be determined with certainty; the two cover distinct phases.
choices.D: Temperate damages are awarded to punish physicians who are grossly negligent.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court held that in cases where the injury is continuing, the award should compensate for pecuniary loss incurred and proved up to trial, and also meet pecuniary loss certain to be suffered but which could not be made with certainty: "temperate damages can and should be awarded on top of actual or compensatory damages in instances where the injury is chronic and continuing," with no incompatibility because "these damages cover two distinct phases." **A is wrong:** the Court tied temperate damages to the chronic injury, not to moral damages. **B is wrong:** temperate damages were added to, not substituted for, the actual damages. **D is wrong:** punishment by way of example is the role of exemplary damages. **Bar trap:** in the 2002 resolution the Court deleted the temperate damages after Erlinda died, since the actual damages already covered her medical expenses.

source.caseTitle: Ramos, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Ruling, the award of temperate damages
source.excerpt: In these cases, the amount of damages which should be awarded, if they are to adequately and correctly respond to the injury caused, should be one which compensates for pecuniary loss incurred and proved, up to the time of trial; and one which would meet pecuniary loss certain to be suffered but which could not, from the nature of the case, be made with certainty. In other words, temperate damages can and should be awarded on top of actual or compensatory damages in instances where the injury is chronic and continuing. And because of the unique nature of such cases, no incompatibility arises when both actual and temperate damages are provided for. The reason is that these damages cover two distinct phases.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: According to Ramos v. Court of Appeals (1999), is the application of res ipsa loquitur in a medical negligence case a question of fact or of law?

choices.A: A question of fact, to be decided only by the medical experts.
choices.B: A question of law, since it is a judicial function to determine whether a certain set of circumstances does, as a matter of law, permit a given inference.
choices.C: A question of fact, to be decided by the hospital's ethics committee.
choices.D: Neither, since res ipsa loquitur is not available in medical cases.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court said: "The application of res ipsa loquitur in medical negligence cases presents a question of law since it is a judicial function to determine whether a certain set of circumstances does, as a matter of law, permit a given inference." **A and C are wrong:** whether the inference is permitted is for the court, not for experts or a hospital committee. **D is wrong:** the Court expressly said medical malpractice cases do not escape the doctrine. **Bar trap:** the facts are proved by evidence, but whether those facts allow the inference of negligence is a legal question for the court.

source.caseTitle: Ramos, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Ruling, res ipsa loquitur in medical negligence cases
source.excerpt: Medical malpractice cases do not escape the application of this doctrine. Thus, res ipsa loquitur has been applied when the circumstances attendant upon the harm are themselves of such a character as to justify an inference of negligence as the cause of that harm. The application of res ipsa loquitur in medical negligence cases presents a question of law since it is a judicial function to determine whether a certain set of circumstances does, as a matter of law, permit a given inference.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Nora complained of weakness, frequent urination, thirst and on-and-off vaginal bleeding. Her doctors scheduled a dilatation and curettage (D&C) to find the cause of the bleeding. The preliminary laboratory results showed a high blood sugar, but without waiting for the full results, and without consulting an internist, they proceeded with the D&C. Nora's diabetes worsened after the operation and she died. Sued by her family, the doctors argue that D&C is the accepted procedure for vaginal bleeding, that their concern was only the bleeding, and that at most they made an honest mistake of judgment. Are the doctors liable? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. The procedure was proper, but proceeding with it, despite the known risk of diabetes and without preparing the patient, fell below the standard of care, and it led to her death.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Flores v. Pineda, the Court held that if a patient suffers from some disability that increases the magnitude of risk to him, that disability must be taken into account so long as it is or should have been known to the physician, and the physician must take commensurate and adequate precautions. Where a D&C is done to diagnose bleeding that is not profuse, it is an elective procedure, and in an elective procedure the physician must conduct a thorough pre-operative evaluation to prepare the patient and minimize risks; the prudent move is to address the patient's hyperglycemia before any other procedure.
suggestedAnswer.application: Nora's weakness, frequent urination and thirst are classic symptoms of diabetes, and the preliminary results showed high blood sugar. Diabetes and its complications were foreseeable. Since the bleeding did not require an emergency operation, the doctors had time to wait for the full results, control her blood sugar and consult an internist. Their claim that their concern was only the bleeding is the very narrow, self-serving view the Court rejected.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The doctors are liable. **Bar trap:** the issue is not whether D&C was a proper procedure (it was) but whether it was proper to do it then, on that patient; a correct procedure done at the wrong time on an unprepared high-risk patient is negligence, not an honest mistake of judgment.

keyPoints: A disability that increases the patient's risk must be taken into account if known or should have been known
Classic diabetes symptoms and a high preliminary blood sugar made the risk foreseeable
The D&C was elective, not an emergency, so a thorough pre-operative evaluation was required
Hyperglycemia should have been controlled first, with an internist
"Our concern was only the bleeding" is a narrow, self-serving view

source.caseTitle: Spouses Flores v. Spouses Pineda, et al.
source.part: The Court's Ruling, Standard of Care and Breach of Duty
source.excerpt: The petitioner spouses' contentions, in our view, miss several points. First, as early as April 17, 1987, Teresita was already suspected to be suffering from diabetes. This suspicion again arose right before the D&C operation on April 28, 1987 when the laboratory result revealed Teresita's increased blood sugar level. Unfortunately, the petitioner spouses did not wait for the full medical laboratory results before proceeding with the D&C, a fact that was never considered in the courts below. Second, the petitioner spouses were duly advised that the patient was experiencing general body weakness, loss of appetite, frequent urination, and thirst - all of which are classic symptoms of diabetes. … Third, the petitioner spouses cannot claim that their principal concern was the vaginal bleeding and should not therefore be held accountable for complications coming from other sources. This is a very narrow and self-serving view that even reflects on their competence. Taken together, we find that reasonable prudence would have shown that diabetes and its complications were foreseeable harm that should have been taken into consideration by the petitioner spouses. If a patient suffers from some disability that increases the magnitude of risk to him, that disability must be taken into account so long as it is or should have been known to the physician. And when the patient is exposed to an increased risk, it is incumbent upon the physician to take commensurate and adequate precautions. … That the D&C operation was conducted principally to diagnose the cause of the vaginal bleeding further leads us to conclude that it was merely an elective procedure, not an emergency case. In an elective procedure, the physician must conduct a thorough pre-operative evaluation of the patient in order to adequately prepare her for the operation and minimize possible risks and complications. … The prudent move is to address the patient's hyperglycemic state immediately and promptly before any other procedure is undertaken.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Explain the elements of duty and breach of duty in a medical negligence case. Who has the burden of proving the elements, by what quantum of evidence, and why is expert testimony generally essential?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Duty refers to the standard of behavior which imposes restrictions on one's conduct; for a physician, the standard is the amount of competence associated with the proper discharge of the profession, at least the level of care that any other reasonably competent doctor would use under the same circumstances. Breach of duty occurs when the physician fails to comply with these professional standards. The plaintiff has the burden of proving the elements by preponderance of evidence, generally through expert testimony.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Flores v. Pineda, the Court described a medical negligence case as a claim to redress a wrong by a medical professional that has caused bodily harm to or the death of a patient, with four elements: duty, breach, injury and proximate causation. As in any civil action, the plaintiff must prove by preponderance of evidence that the physician failed to do what a reasonably prudent health care provider would have done, or did what one would not have done, and that this caused injury. Expert testimony is essential because whether a physician exercised the requisite skill and care is generally a matter of expert opinion.
suggestedAnswer.application: So a patient's family must show, usually through qualified doctors, what a reasonably competent physician would have done in the same circumstances, that the defendant departed from it, and that the departure caused the injury or death. In Flores, the family's experts testified that the D&C should have been postponed and the diabetes managed by an internist first.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Duty is the professional standard of competence; breach is the failure to meet it; the plaintiff proves both by preponderance of evidence, generally through experts. **Bar trap:** a civil medical negligence case needs only preponderance of evidence, not proof beyond reasonable doubt (compare Jarcia v. People).

keyPoints: Elements: duty, breach, injury, proximate causation
Duty: the standard of behavior restricting one's conduct; at least the care of a reasonably competent doctor in the same circumstances
Breach: failure to comply with the professional standards
Burden on the plaintiff, by preponderance of evidence
Expert testimony is essential, since skill and care are generally a matter of expert opinion

source.caseTitle: Spouses Flores v. Spouses Pineda, et al.
source.part: The Court's Ruling, Elements of a Medical Negligence Case
source.excerpt: A medical negligence case is a type of claim to redress a wrong committed by a medical professional, that has caused bodily harm to or the death of a patient. There are four elements involved in a medical negligence case, namely: duty, breach, injury, and proximate causation. Duty refers to the standard of behavior which imposes restrictions on one's conduct. The standard in turn refers to the amount of competence associated with the proper discharge of the profession. A physician is expected to use at least the same level of care that any other reasonably competent doctor would use under the same circumstances. Breach of duty occurs when the physician fails to comply with these professional standards. If injury results to the patient as a result of this breach, the physician is answerable for negligence. As in any civil action, the burden to prove the existence of the necessary elements rests with the plaintiff. To successfully pursue a claim, the plaintiff must prove by preponderance of evidence that, one, the physician either failed to do something which a reasonably prudent health care provider would have done, or that he did something that a reasonably prudent provider would not have done; and two, the failure or action caused injury to the patient. Expert testimony is therefore essential since the factual issue of whether a physician or surgeon has exercised the requisite degree of skill and care in the treatment of his patient is generally a matter of expert opinion.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In a suit against doctors who operated on a patient with uncontrolled high blood sugar, the doctors argue that the patient died of diabetes, a disease they did not cause, and that nothing shows her death could have been averted by other means. Discuss how causation must be proved in a medical negligence case, and resolve the argument.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Causation is the critical and clinching factor: the plaintiff must prove that the defendant's fault caused the injury, within a reasonable medical probability based on competent expert testimony, not speculation. Here causation is proved: the operation, done without first controlling the diabetes, aggravated it and led to death.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Flores v. Pineda, the Court held that the plaintiff must plead and prove not only that he had been injured and that the defendant was at fault, but also that the defendant's fault caused the injury; a verdict in a malpractice action cannot be based on speculation or conjecture, and causation must be proven within a reasonable medical probability based upon competent expert testimony.
suggestedAnswer.application: The expert testimony explained that surgical stress makes a diabetic's body secrete counter-regulatory hormones, causing prolonged hyperglycemia that, if unchecked, can lead to death; the death certificate listed ketoacidosis with diabetes as the underlying cause; and after the D&C the patient's blood sugar shot up. Between the D&C and death was a diabetic complication that could have been prevented with standard precautions. That the doctors did not cause the diabetes does not matter; their operation on an unprepared diabetic aggravated it.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The argument fails; the causal link between the negligent D&C and the death was sufficiently established. **Bar trap:** the defendant need not have caused the underlying disease; it is enough that his negligence aggravated a known risk and produced the death.

keyPoints: Causation is the critical and clinching factor in a medical negligence case
The plaintiff must prove injury, fault, and that the fault caused the injury
No verdict on speculation; causation within a reasonable medical probability, through competent expert testimony
Surgical stress aggravated the diabetes, leading to ketoacidosis and death
The doctors need not have caused the disease; their negligence aggravated it

source.caseTitle: Spouses Flores v. Spouses Pineda, et al.
source.part: The Court's Ruling, Injury and Causation
source.excerpt: As previously mentioned, the critical and clinching factor in a medical negligence case is proof of the causal connection between the negligence which the evidence established and the plaintiff's injuries; the plaintiff must plead and prove not only that he had been injured and defendant has been at fault, but also that the defendant's fault caused the injury. A verdict in a malpractice action cannot be based on speculation or conjecture. Causation must be proven within a reasonable medical probability based upon competent expert testimony. … Stress, whether physical or emotional, is a factor that can aggravate diabetes; a D&C operation is a form of physical stress. Dr. Mendoza explained how surgical stress can aggravate the patient's hyperglycemia: when stress occurs, the diabetic's body, especially the autonomic system, reacts by secreting hormones which are counter-regulatory; she can have prolonged hyperglycemia which, if unchecked, could lead to death. … Thus, between the D&C and death was the diabetic complication that could have been prevented with the observance of standard medical precautions.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Flores v. Pineda, "the standard of behavior which imposes restrictions on one's conduct" is the Court's definition of

choices.A: breach.
choices.B: proximate causation.
choices.C: duty.
choices.D: injury.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court said: "Duty refers to the standard of behavior which imposes restrictions on one's conduct. The standard in turn refers to the amount of competence associated with the proper discharge of the profession." **A is wrong:** breach of duty occurs when the physician fails to comply with these professional standards. **B is wrong:** proximate causation is the link between the breach and the injury. **D is wrong:** injury is the harm the patient suffers. **Bar trap:** know each of the four elements by its own definition.

source.caseTitle: Spouses Flores v. Spouses Pineda, et al.
source.part: The Court's Ruling, Elements of a Medical Negligence Case
source.excerpt: Duty refers to the standard of behavior which imposes restrictions on one's conduct. The standard in turn refers to the amount of competence associated with the proper discharge of the profession. A physician is expected to use at least the same level of care that any other reasonably competent doctor would use under the same circumstances. Breach of duty occurs when the physician fails to comply with these professional standards.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: The doctors in Flores v. Pineda claimed they performed the D&C urgently because the patient's vaginal bleeding was profuse. Why did the Court not believe them?

choices.A: Because their testimonies were self-serving and inconsistent, and the medical records did not indicate profuse bleeding although it was the main complaint; a medical record that does not indicate it "speaks loudly and clearly of what it does not contain."
choices.B: Because profuse bleeding never justifies a D&C.
choices.C: Because the patient herself denied any bleeding.
choices.D: Because only the hospital director may certify that a case is an emergency.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court declined to rely on the claim because it was self-serving and the doctors were inconsistent (one testified he saw the bleeding, then that he did not). The experts testified that the records failed to show profuse bleeding, which was odd since bleeding was the main complaint; a medical record is the only long-term transcription of patient care, and one "that does not indicate profuse medical bleeding speaks loudly and clearly of what it does not contain." **B is wrong:** the experts said a D&C on a hyperglycemic patient may be justified in an emergency, when there is profuse bleeding. **C is wrong:** the patient did complain of on-and-off bleeding. **D is wrong:** no such rule figures in the case. **Bar trap:** what is missing from the medical record can be evidence against the doctor.

source.caseTitle: Spouses Flores v. Spouses Pineda, et al.
source.part: The Court's Ruling, Standard of Care and Breach of Duty (the medical records)
source.excerpt: In this case, we choose not to rely on the assertions of the petitioner spouses that there was profuse bleeding, not only because the statements were self-serving, but also because the petitioner spouses were inconsistent in their testimonies. … Dr. Tan and Dr. Mendoza both testified that the medical records of Teresita failed to indicate that there was profuse vaginal bleeding. The claim that there was profuse vaginal bleeding although this was not reflected in the medical records strikes us as odd since the main complaint is vaginal bleeding. A medical record is the only document that maintains a long-term transcription of patient care and as such, its maintenance is considered a priority in hospital practice. Optimal record-keeping includes all patient inter-actions. The records should always be clear, objective, and up-to-date. Thus, a medical record that does not indicate profuse medical bleeding speaks loudly and clearly of what it does not contain.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Flores v. Pineda, the Court added an award that the Court of Appeals had missed. Which award, and on what basis?

choices.A: Temperate damages, because the patient's illness was chronic and continuing.
choices.B: Nominal damages, because the heirs' rights were violated.
choices.C: Liquidated damages, because the hospital's admission form fixed them.
choices.D: ₱50,000 death indemnity under Article 2206 of the Civil Code, which provides damages for death caused by a quasi-delict "even though there may have been mitigating circumstances."

questions.explanation: **D is correct.** The Court held that the heirs were entitled to ₱50,000 as death indemnity under Article 2206 of the Civil Code, which states that the amount of damages for death caused by a quasi-delict shall be at least a fixed sum "even though there may have been mitigating circumstances," and called this "a question of law that the CA missed in its decision." The same article allows moral damages for death by quasi-delict to the spouse and ascendants or descendants. **A, B and C are wrong:** none of these was awarded or discussed in the decision. **Bar trap:** death indemnity is separate from, and in addition to, actual, moral and exemplary damages.

source.caseTitle: Spouses Flores v. Spouses Pineda, et al.
source.part: The Court's Ruling, Award of Damages (death indemnity)
source.excerpt: In addition to the award for actual damages, the respondent heirs of Teresita are likewise entitled to P50,000.00 as death indemnity pursuant to Article 2206 of the Civil Code, which states that "the amount of damages for death caused by a xxx quasi-delict shall be at least three thousand pesos, even though there may have been mitigating circumstances xxx." This is a question of law that the CA missed in its decision and which we now decide in the respondents' favor.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: According to Flores v. Pineda, when a patient suffers from some disability that increases the magnitude of risk to him, what must the physician do?

choices.A: Nothing beyond the procedure requested, since the physician is responsible only for the complaint presented.
choices.B: Take the disability into account so long as it is or should have been known to him, and take commensurate and adequate precautions.
choices.C: Refuse to treat the patient altogether.
choices.D: Proceed, but only after the patient signs a waiver of liability.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court held: "If a patient suffers from some disability that increases the magnitude of risk to him, that disability must be taken into account so long as it is or should have been known to the physician. And when the patient is exposed to an increased risk, it is incumbent upon the physician to take commensurate and adequate precautions." **A is wrong:** the Court called the doctors' focus on the bleeding alone "a very narrow and self-serving view." **C is wrong:** the duty is to take precautions (here, control the blood sugar and consult an internist), not to refuse treatment. **D is wrong:** no waiver figures in the decision. **Bar trap:** "should have been known" means the physician is charged with risks that the symptoms or tests point to, even if not yet confirmed.

source.caseTitle: Spouses Flores v. Spouses Pineda, et al.
source.part: The Court's Ruling, Standard of Care and Breach of Duty (increased risk)
source.excerpt: If a patient suffers from some disability that increases the magnitude of risk to him, that disability must be taken into account so long as it is or should have been known to the physician. And when the patient is exposed to an increased risk, it is incumbent upon the physician to take commensurate and adequate precautions.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Dr. Fredelicto Flores, an anesthesiologist, argued in Flores v. Pineda that he could not be liable for the D&C, which was performed by his wife, an obstetrician-gynecologist. On what ground did the Court hold him liable?

choices.A: Because spouses are always solidarily liable for each other's professional acts.
choices.B: Because an anesthesiologist is always the captain of the ship.
choices.C: Because he failed from the start to identify and confirm diabetes as a risk factor despite the complaints and his own suspicions, and he took part in the imprudent decision to proceed despite the early laboratory results.
choices.D: Because he administered the wrong anesthetic drug.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court clarified that his negligence was "his failure from the very start to identify and confirm, despite the patient's complaints and his own suspicions, that diabetes was a risk factor that should be guarded against, and his participation in the imprudent decision to proceed with the D&C operation despite his early suspicion and the confirmatory early laboratory results." If he considered himself incompetent to treat the diabetes, he should also have refrained from deciding to proceed, not being an obstetrician or gynecologist. **A is wrong:** liability rested on his own negligence, not on the marriage. **B is wrong:** the decision does not apply the captain of the ship rule to him. **D is wrong:** no wrong drug was found. **Bar trap:** a doctor who joins a decision outside his specialty shares responsibility for it.

source.caseTitle: Spouses Flores v. Spouses Pineda, et al.
source.part: The Court's Ruling, Injury and Causation (the liability of Dr. Fredelicto)
source.excerpt: However, we clarify that Dr. Fredelicto's negligence is not solely the act of ordering an "on call" D&C operation when he was mainly an anaesthesiologist who had made a very cursory examination of the patient's vaginal bleeding complaint. Rather, it was his failure from the very start to identify and confirm, despite the patient's complaints and his own suspicions, that diabetes was a risk factor that should be guarded against, and his participation in the imprudent decision to proceed with the D&C operation despite his early suspicion and the confirmatory early laboratory results.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Discuss the doctrine of informed consent. What must a physician disclose, how much explanation is required, and are there exceptions?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Informed consent is the principle that a physician has a duty to disclose what a reasonably prudent physician in the medical community, exercising reasonable care, would disclose to his patient about the grave risks of injury from a proposed treatment, so that the patient, faced with a choice of undergoing it, an alternative treatment, or none at all, may intelligently exercise his judgment by balancing the probable risks against the probable benefits.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Li v. Soliman, the Court traced the doctrine from the tort of battery for treatment without consent, through Justice Cardozo's statement in Schloendorff that every adult of sound mind has a right to determine what shall be done with his own body. Following Canterbury v. Spence, the duty to warn is part of the physician's responsibility, since patients are ordinarily unlearned in medicine; but it requires only a reasonable explanation in nontechnical terms of what is at stake: the therapy alternatives, the goals expectably to be achieved, and the risks of treatment or no treatment, not a short medical education. Following Cobbs v. Grant, the physician need not discuss relatively minor risks of very low incidence in common procedures; the exceptions are emergencies where the patient evidently cannot evaluate data, and where the patient is a child or incompetent. The test for what must be divulged is its materiality to the patient's decision.
suggestedAnswer.application: A doctor recommending chemotherapy must therefore explain in plain terms the goals of the treatment, the alternatives (including no treatment), and its material risks, such as the drugs' effects on the blood counts and organs, so the patient or the parents can decide. Statistical data may not be legally necessary.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Informed consent requires a reasonable, nontechnical disclosure of material risks and alternatives, measured by what is material to the patient's decision. **Bar trap:** the duty is not to disclose every conceivable risk; minor, very rare risks of common procedures need not be discussed.

keyPoints: Duty to disclose what a reasonably prudent physician would disclose about the grave risks of a proposed treatment

source.caseTitle: Li v. Spouses Soliman
source.part: Ruling, the doctrine of informed consent
source.excerpt: From a purely ethical norm, informed consent evolved into a general principle of law that a physician has a duty to disclose what a reasonably prudent physician in the medical community in the exercise of reasonable care would disclose to his patient as to whatever grave risks of injury might be incurred from a proposed course of treatment, so that a patient, exercising ordinary care for his own welfare, and faced with a choice of undergoing the proposed treatment, or alternative treatment, or none at all, may intelligently exercise his judgment by reasonably balancing the probable risks against the probable benefits. … The physician is not expected to give the patient a short medical education, the disclosure rule only requires of him a reasonable explanation, which means generally informing the patient in nontechnical terms as to what is at stake; the therapy alternatives open to him, the goals expectably to be achieved, and the risks that may ensue from particular treatment or no treatment. … However, the physician is not obliged to discuss relatively minor risks inherent in common procedures when it is common knowledge that such risks inherent in procedure of very low incidence. Cited as exceptions to the rule that the patient should not be denied the opportunity to weigh the risks of surgery or treatment are emergency cases where it is evident he cannot evaluate data, and where the patient is a child or incompetent. The court thus concluded that the patient’s right of self-decision can only be effectively exercised if the patient possesses adequate information to enable him in making an intelligent choice. The scope of the physician’s communications to the patient, then must be measured by the patient’s need, and that need is whatever information is material to the decision. The test therefore for determining whether a potential peril must be divulged is its materiality to the patient’s decision.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: What are the essential elements that a plaintiff must prove in a malpractice action based on the doctrine of informed consent? Explain the element of causation in such an action.

suggestedAnswer.answer: There are four: (1) the physician had a duty to disclose material risks; (2) he failed to disclose or inadequately disclosed those risks; (3) as a direct and proximate result of the failure to disclose, the patient consented to treatment she otherwise would not have consented to; and (4) the plaintiff was injured by the proposed treatment.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Li v. Soliman lists these elements and holds that the gravamen in an informed consent case requires the plaintiff to point to significant undisclosed information relating to the treatment which would have altered her decision to undergo it. Following Canterbury v. Spence and Cobbs v. Grant, the unrevealed risk must also materialize, for otherwise the omission, however unpardonable, is without legal consequence; and there must be a causal relationship between the failure to inform and the injury, which arises only if it is established that, had revelation been made, consent to treatment would not have been given.
suggestedAnswer.application: So it is not enough for the patient to show that some risk was not mentioned. She must show that the risk was material, that it actually came about, and that had it been disclosed she would have refused the treatment, the refusal being what would have spared her the injury.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Duty, failure to disclose, consent that would otherwise not have been given, and injury. **Bar trap:** an omission that did not change the patient's decision, or a risk that never materialized, carries no liability even if the disclosure was incomplete.

keyPoints: (1) Duty to disclose material risks
(2) Failure to disclose, or inadequate disclosure
(3) As a direct and proximate result, the patient consented to treatment she otherwise would not have consented to
(4) Injury from the proposed treatment
The undisclosed risk must materialize, and the information must be significant enough to have altered the decision

source.part: Ruling, the elements of an action based on informed consent
source.excerpt: Such unrevealed risk that should have been made known must further materialize, for otherwise the omission, however unpardonable, is without legal consequence. And, as in malpractice actions generally, there must be a causal relationship between the physician’s failure to divulge and damage to the patient. … Cobbs v. Grant further reiterated the pronouncement in Canterbury v. Spence that for liability of the physician for failure to inform patient, there must be causal relationship between physician’s failure to inform and the injury to patient and such connection arises only if it is established that, had revelation been made, consent to treatment would not have been given. There are four essential elements a plaintiff must prove in a malpractice action based upon the doctrine of informed consent: "(1) the physician had a duty to disclose material risks; (2) he failed to disclose or inadequately disclosed those risks; (3) as a direct and proximate result of the failure to disclose, the patient consented to treatment she otherwise would not have consented to; and (4) plaintiff was injured by the proposed treatment." questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Before chemotherapy for their child's aggressive bone cancer, Dr. Tan told the parents that the drugs would lower the child's white and red blood cells and platelets, could damage the heart and kidneys, and could cause hair loss, vomiting and skin darkening. The child died of complications eleven days after the first cycle. The parents sue Dr. Tan for not telling them that the treatment could cause death. Their only witness on the duty to disclose is a Department of Health medical specialist who handles complaints against hospitals and is not an oncologist. No negligence in the treatment itself is shown. Is Dr. Tan liable? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The disclosure was adequate, and the parents failed to prove the standard of disclosure through a qualified expert.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Li v. Soliman, the Court held that there was adequate disclosure of the material risks of chemotherapy when the parents were told of its general side effects (lowered blood counts, decrease in platelets, possible kidney or heart damage, skin darkening); that death can result from the treatment or the underlying cancer is a risk that cannot be ruled out in most major procedures, but such a conclusion can reasonably be drawn from the side effects already disclosed. It also held that in an action based on lack of informed consent, the plaintiff must prove both the duty and its breach through expert testimony showing the customary standard of care of physicians in the same practice as the defendant; a DOH medical specialist who is not an oncologist does not qualify.
suggestedAnswer.application: The parents knew the child's immune system was already weak from the cancer and were told how the drugs would affect her blood and organs; the reaction of each patient cannot be precisely determined beforehand. From those disclosed effects, the possibility of a fatal outcome could reasonably be drawn. And with no oncologist to establish what disclosure the profession requires, duty and breach were not proved.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Dr. Tan is not liable. **Bar trap:** a doctor need not recite every possible outcome, including death, when it follows from the serious risks already disclosed; and in Li the Court required expert testimony from the same field to prove the duty to disclose; Que v. Philippine Heart Center (2025) restated the Li doctrine and likewise required an expert who is a similarly trained and experienced physician.

keyPoints: Disclosure of the general side effects of chemotherapy was adequate
The possibility of death can reasonably be drawn from the serious side effects disclosed
Each patient's reaction cannot be precisely determined beforehand
Under Li, duty and breach must be proved by expert testimony of physicians in the same practice
A non-oncologist DOH specialist is not a qualified expert on the standard of disclosure for chemotherapy

source.caseTitle: Li v. Spouses Soliman
source.part: Ruling, adequate disclosure and the need for expert testimony
source.excerpt: Examining the evidence on record, we hold that there was adequate disclosure of material risks inherent in the chemotherapy procedure performed with the consent of Angelica’s parents. Respondents could not have been unaware in the course of initial treatment and amputation of Angelica’s lower extremity, that her immune system was already weak on account of the malignant tumor in her knee. When petitioner informed the respondents beforehand of the side effects of chemotherapy which includes lowered counts of white and red blood cells, decrease in blood platelets, possible kidney or heart damage and skin darkening, there is reasonable expectation on the part of the doctor that the respondents understood very well that the severity of these side effects will not be the same for all patients undergoing the procedure. In other words, by the nature of the disease itself, each patient’s reaction to the chemical agents even with pre-treatment laboratory tests cannot be precisely determined by the physician. That death can possibly result from complications of the treatment or the underlying cancer itself, immediately or sometime after the administration of chemotherapy drugs, is a risk that cannot be ruled out, as with most other major medical procedures, but such conclusion can be reasonably drawn from the general side effects of chemotherapy already disclosed. … Further, in a medical malpractice action based on lack of informed consent, "the plaintiff must prove both the duty and the breach of that duty through expert testimony. Such expert testimony must show the customary standard of care of physicians in the same practice as that of the defendant doctor. In this case, the testimony of Dr. Balmaceda who is not an oncologist but a Medical Specialist of the DOH’s Operational and Management Services charged with receiving complaints against hospitals, does not qualify as expert testimony to establish the standard of care in obtaining consent for chemotherapy treatment.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A surgeon, sued together with the anesthesiologist he recommended for a patient's brain damage during intubation, argues that anesthesiology and surgery are distinct specialties, that he had no control over the anesthesiologist, and that courts in the United States have abandoned the captain of the ship doctrine. The evidence shows that he had always worked with this anesthesiologist, recommended her to the patient, admitted being the attending physician, watched the intubation and noticed the patient's bluish nails, and arrived three hours late for the scheduled operation. Is the surgeon liable? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. The trend abroad does not bind Philippine courts, and on these facts the surgeon exercised at least supervision and worked with the anesthesiologist as a team; his three-hour delay was also a breach of his own duty.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In its 2002 resolution in Ramos v. Court of Appeals, the Court held that a trend in American jurisprudence to do away with the captain of the ship doctrine does not mean that the Court will ipso facto follow it; the peculiar facts justified applying it. The surgeon recommended the anesthesiologist (representing her competence), was the attending physician, and worked with her as a team whose duties intersect, so they were not completely independent of each other as to absolve one from the other's negligence. Arriving more than three hours late, after double-booking, subjected the patient to continued starvation and aggravated anxiety, which affects the administration of anesthesia; this violated his duty to serve his patients with the greatest solicitude and Article 19 of the Civil Code, which requires one to act with justice and give everyone his due.
suggestedAnswer.application: The surgeon's own acts (recommending the anesthesiologist, being the attending physician, keeping an eye on the intubation, calling for help when the patient turned blue) show supervision and teamwork, not separate watertight compartments. His lateness was an independent breach. Specialization does not excuse him on these facts.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The surgeon is liable with the anesthesiologist. **Bar trap:** the captain of the ship doctrine is applied on the facts; the Court did not adopt the American trend to abandon it, but it relied on actual supervision and teamwork, not on title alone.

They worked as a team with intersecting duties; not completely independent
