source.caseTitle: Ramos, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al. (Resolution)
source.part: Resolution, the liability of Dr. Hosaka (captain of the ship)
source.excerpt: That there is a trend in American jurisprudence to do away with the Captain-of-the-Ship doctrine does not mean that this Court will ipso facto follow said trend. Due regard for the peculiar factual circumstances obtaining in this case justify the application of the Captain-of-the-Ship doctrine. From the facts on record it can be logically inferred that Dr. Hosaka exercised a certain degree of, at the very least, supervision over the procedure then being performed on Erlinda. First, it was Dr. Hosaka who recommended to petitioners the services of Dr. Gutierrez. In effect, he represented to petitioners that Dr. Gutierrez possessed the necessary competence and skills. … Second, Dr. Hosaka himself admitted that he was the attending physician of Erlinda. … Third, it is conceded that in performing their responsibilities to the patient, Drs. Hosaka and Gutierrez worked as a team. Their work cannot be placed in separate watertight compartments because their duties intersect with each other. While the professional services of Dr. Hosaka and Dr. Gutierrez were secured primarily for their performance of acts within their respective fields of expertise for the treatment of petitioner Erlinda, and that one does not exercise control over the other, they were certainly not completely independent of each other so as to absolve one from the negligent acts of the other physician. … Dr. Hosaka's irresponsible conduct of arriving very late for the scheduled operation of petitioner Erlinda is violative, not only of his duty as a physician "to serve the interest of his patients with the greatest solicitude, giving them always his best talent and skill," but also of Article 19 of the Civil Code which requires a person, in the performance of his duties, to act with justice and give everyone his due.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Is a private hospital solidarily liable under Article 2180 of the Civil Code for the negligence of its visiting consultant surgeon and anesthesiologist, on the ground that hospitals hire, fire and control their consultants? Explain, with reference to the 2002 resolution in Ramos v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Not on that ground alone. In its 2002 resolution the Court reversed its 1999 holding and absolved the hospital, finding no employer-employee relationship between it and the consultant doctors under the four-fold test, and no failure of the hospital's own facilities or staff.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: An employer-employee relationship requires: (1) the selection and engagement of services; (2) the payment of wages; (3) the power to hire and fire; and (4) the power to control not only the end to be achieved but the means to be used in reaching it. In Ramos (2002), the Court found that consultants are admitted to the medical staff through a credentials committee of department heads, disciplined through an ethics committee of specialty heads, and not paid by the hospital; and that the contract between the consultant and the patient (for medical services) is separate and distinct from the contract between the hospital and the patient (for facilities and services of its staff). No evidence showed the injury was due to a failure of the hospital to provide facilities and staff.
suggestedAnswer.application: The hospital therefore did not answer under Article 2180 for the doctors' negligence; only the two doctors were held solidarily liable. A hospital may still be liable on other grounds where the facts support them (for example, apparent authority or its own corporate negligence, as later discussed in Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana), but those were not the basis of the 1999 ruling that was reversed.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The hospital was absolved for lack of an employer-employee relationship. **Bar trap:** do not cite the 1999 Ramos pronouncement that an employer-employee relationship "in effect" exists between hospitals and consultants; it was reversed in 2002.

keyPoints: Four-fold test: selection and engagement; payment of wages; power to dismiss; power of control over the means
Consultants are admitted by a credentials committee and disciplined by an ethics committee of department heads
The hospital does not pay the consultants
Contract between consultant and patient (medical services) is distinct from hospital and patient (facilities and staff)
No failure of the hospital's own facilities or staff was shown; the hospital was absolved

source.caseTitle: Ramos, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al. (Resolution)
source.part: Resolution, the liability of DLSMC
source.excerpt: It has been consistently held that in determining whether an employer-employee relationship exists between the parties, the following elements must be present: (1) selection and engagement of services; (2) payment of wages; (3) the power to hire and fire; and (4) the power to control not only the end to be achieved, but the means to be used in reaching such an end. … After a careful consideration of the arguments raised by DLSMC, the Court finds that respondent hospital’s position on this issue is meritorious. There is no employer-employee relationship between DLSMC and Drs. Gutierrez and Hosaka which would hold DLSMC solidarily liable for the injury suffered by petitioner Erlinda under Article 2180 of the Civil Code. As explained by respondent hospital, that the admission of a physician to membership in DLSMC’s medical staff as active or visiting consultant is first decided upon by the Credentials Committee thereof, which is composed of the heads of the various specialty departments such as the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Pediatrics, Surgery with the department head of the particular specialty applied for as chairman. … Neither is there any showing that it is DLSMC which pays any of its consultants for medical services rendered by the latter to their respective patients. Moreover, the contract between the consultant in respondent hospital and his patient is separate and distinct from the contract between respondent hospital and said patient. The first has for its object the rendition of medical services by the consultant to the patient, while the second concerns the provision by the hospital of facilities and services by its staff such as nurses and laboratory personnel necessary for the proper treatment of the patient. Further, no evidence was adduced to show that the injury suffered by petitioner Erlinda was due to a failure on the part of respondent DLSMC to provide for hospital facilities and staff necessary for her treatment. For these reasons, we reverse the finding of liability on the part of DLSMC for the injury suffered by petitioner Erlinda.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: An anesthesiologist argues that a full pre-anesthetic evaluation is needed only in elective operations, and that since she listened to the patient's heart and lungs and took her blood pressure an hour before the operation, she did all that was required. Under the 2002 resolution in Ramos v. Court of Appeals, is she correct? Explain what a pre-anesthetic evaluation involves.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. A pre-anesthetic evaluation, whether the operation is elective or an emergency, cannot be dispensed with; and checking the heart, lungs and blood pressure without examining the patient's airway is not a thorough evaluation.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In its 2002 resolution in Ramos, the Court, guided by the anesthesiologists who appeared as amici curiae, held that the conduct of a preanesthetic or preoperative evaluation prior to an operation, whether elective or emergency, cannot be dispensed with, since it is necessary to formulate a plan of anesthesia care suited to the patient. It involves taking the medical history, reviewing current drug therapy, conducting a physical examination, interpreting laboratory data, and determining the appropriate preoperative medications. The physical examination covers the central nervous system, cardiovascular system and lungs, and also the upper airway (cervical spine and jaw mobility, prominent incisors, diseased or artificial teeth, the uvula and the thyromental distance).
suggestedAnswer.application: The anesthesiologist saw the patient only an hour before the operation and did not examine her airway. Had she done so, she would most probably not have had difficulty intubating the patient, and the injury could have been avoided. Her partial check does not meet the standard.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: She is not correct; she was negligent. **Bar trap:** the 1999 decision stressed that elective cases leave ample time for evaluation; the 2002 resolution goes further: the evaluation cannot be dispensed with in either elective or emergency operations.

keyPoints: A pre-anesthetic evaluation cannot be dispensed with, whether the operation is elective or an emergency
Purpose: a plan of anesthesia care suited to the patient
It covers medical history, current drug therapy, physical examination, laboratory data, preoperative medications
The physical examination includes the upper airway
Failing to examine the airway led to the difficult intubation and the injury

source.caseTitle: Ramos, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al. (Resolution)
source.part: Resolution, the liability of Dr. Gutierrez (pre-anesthetic evaluation)
source.excerpt: The conduct of a preanesthetic/preoperative evaluation prior to an operation, whether elective or emergency, cannot be dispensed with. Such evaluation is necessary for the formulation of a plan of anesthesia care suited to the needs of the patient concerned. Pre-evaluation for anesthesia involves taking the patient’s medical history, reviewing his current drug therapy, conducting physical examination, interpreting laboratory data, and determining the appropriate prescription of preoperative medications as necessary to the conduct of anesthesia. Physical examination of the patient entails not only evaluating the patient’s central nervous system, cardiovascular system and lungs but also the upper airway. Examination of the upper airway would in turn include an analysis of the patient’s cervical spine mobility, temporomandibular mobility, prominent central incisors, deceased or artificial teeth, ability to visualize uvula and the thyromental distance. Nonetheless, Dr. Gutierrez omitted to perform a thorough preoperative evaluation on Erlinda. As she herself admitted, she saw Erlinda for the first time on the day of the operation itself, one hour before the scheduled operation. She auscultated the patient’s heart and lungs and checked the latter’s blood pressure to determine if Erlinda was indeed fit for operation. However, she did not proceed to examine the patient’s airway. Had she been able to check petitioner Erlinda’s airway prior to the operation, Dr. Gutierrez would most probably not have experienced difficulty in intubating the former, and thus the resultant injury could have been avoided.

It also noted that, being a nurse and a nursing dean, she was not entirely ignorant of anesthetic procedure. **B is wrong:** no such rule exists. **C is wrong:** others, including nurses and doctors, were present. **D is wrong:** this was not the Court's reason. **Bar trap:** under res ipsa loquitur, a non-expert's testimony on what anyone can observe suffices.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: After Dr. Lacson performed a hysterectomy on Carla, Carla suffered recurring fever and vomiting. Three months later another doctor removed a foul-smelling rolled gauze from her cervix. Carla had undergone no other operation. Sued for damages, Dr. Lacson points to the hospital record showing that the surgical sponge count was complete, and argues that no gauze could have been left by her. Is Dr. Lacson liable? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. Leaving a gauze in the patient after closing the incision is at least prima facie negligence of the operating surgeon, and the surgeon must personally see to it that the counts are correct; the circumstances leave no other likely source of the gauze.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Mendoza v. Casumpang, the Court, quoting Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana, held that an operation requiring sponges is not complete until they are properly removed, and that leaving sponges or other foreign substances in the wound after the incision has been closed is at least prima facie negligence by the operating surgeon, even negligence per se. It added that a surgical operation is the responsibility of the surgeon performing it, who must personally ascertain that the counts of instruments and materials used before the surgery and before sewing the patient up have been correctly done.
suggestedAnswer.application: Carla had no other surgery, and it is most unlikely that she, or any woman, would put a roll of gauze into her own cervix. The gauze found after Dr. Lacson's operation thus raises an inference of her negligence. A record of a complete sponge count does not overcome it, since the surgeon herself was responsible for making sure the count was right.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Dr. Lacson is liable for damages. **Bar trap:** "the hospital's sponge count was complete" does not shift the responsibility; the operating surgeon must personally ascertain the count.

keyPoints: Leaving a sponge or gauze after closing is at least prima facie negligence (even negligence per se) of the operating surgeon
The operation is not complete until all sponges are removed
The surgeon must personally ascertain that the counts are correct
No other surgery, and no plausible other source of the gauze

source.caseTitle: Mendoza v. Casumpang, et al.
source.part: Decision, the liability of Dr. Mendoza
source.excerpt: As the RTC pointed out, Josephine did not undergo any other surgical operation. And it would be much unlikely for her or for any woman to inject a roll of gauze into her cervix. As the Court held in Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana: An operation requiring the placing of sponges in the incision is not complete until the sponges are properly removed, and it is settled that the leaving of sponges or other foreign substances in the wound after the incision has been closed is at least prima facie negligence by the operating surgeon. To put it simply, such act is considered so inconsistent with due care as to raise an inference of negligence. There are even legions of authorities to the effect that such act is negligence per se. … A surgical operation is the responsibility of the surgeon performing it. He must personally ascertain that the counts of instruments and materials used before the surgery and prior to sewing the patient up have been correctly done.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A patient died after a surgeon negligently left a gauze inside her. Her heirs were awarded actual damages, moral damages and attorney's fees by the lower courts. What other damages may they recover, and on what basis? Explain, following Mendoza v. Casumpang.

suggestedAnswer.answer: They may also recover exemplary damages and civil indemnity for the death, and the attorney's fees may be increased.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Mendoza v. Casumpang, the Court noted that under Article 2229 of the Civil Code, exemplary damages are imposed by way of example or correction for the public good, in addition to moral damages, and may also be awarded in cases of gross negligence. Because the patient's death resulted from the surgeon's negligence, civil indemnity under Article 2206 should be given to the heirs, in the amount of ₱50,000 fixed by prevailing jurisprudence. It also found it just and equitable under Article 2208 to increase the attorney's fees.
suggestedAnswer.application: To provide an example to the medical profession and to stress the need for constant vigilance in attending to a patient's health, the Court awarded ₱50,000 exemplary damages; it added ₱50,000 civil indemnity for the death, and raised the attorney's fees from ₱20,000 to ₱50,000.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Exemplary damages (Art. 2229), civil indemnity for death (Art. 2206) and increased attorney's fees (Art. 2208). **Bar trap:** exemplary damages are awarded in addition to moral damages, and civil indemnity for death is a separate award, not part of moral or actual damages.

Exemplary damages may be awarded for gross negligence
Civil indemnity for death under Article 2206 (₱50,000 per prevailing jurisprudence at the time)
Attorney's fees increased as just and equitable under Article 2208
Purpose: an example to the medical profession, stressing constant vigilance

Exemplary damages may also be awarded in cases of gross negligence. A surgical operation is the responsibility of the surgeon performing it. He must personally ascertain that the counts of instruments and materials used before the surgery and prior to sewing the patient up have been correctly done. To provide an example to the medical profession and to stress the need for constant vigilance in attending to a patient’s health, the award of exemplary damages in this case is in order. Casumpang, the Court held that the surgeon raised a question of fact at its level, when parties may raise only questions of law in petitions for review on certiorari from the Court of Appeals; with few exceptions, the factual findings of that court are generally binding, and none of the exceptions applied.

The Court of Appeals found that a gauze remained after surgery, and its finding, supported by the absence of any other operation, binds the Supreme Court.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The Supreme Court will not re-examine the claim, and the finding of negligence stands. **Bar trap:** in a Rule 45 petition, an argument about what the evidence shows is a question of fact, not of law, unless an exception applies.

Whether a gauze was left is a question of fact
The Court of Appeals' factual findings are generally binding, with few exceptions

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Mario, who had an aortic aneurysm, chose a less invasive stenting procedure over open surgery after his doctor explained both options, told him the stenting carried risks including death, and told him that a visiting foreign specialist, not he, would perform it. Mario signed two consent forms, which no witness signed. During the procedure he suffered a stroke and died. His son sues the doctor, claiming the family was told the procedure was "virtually risk-free" and that the consent forms are invalid for lack of witnesses. Experts testify that stroke is an inherent risk of stenting. Is the doctor liable for lack of informed consent? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The doctor disclosed the material risks of the procedure, including death, and the consent forms are valid; the missing witnesses' signatures are irrelevant absent proof of forgery or incapacity.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Que v. Philippine Heart Center (2025), the Court, restating Li v. Soliman, held that in a lack of informed consent case the plaintiff must prove: (1) the physician had a duty to disclose material risks; (2) he failed to disclose or inadequately disclosed them; (3) as a direct and proximate result, the patient consented to treatment he otherwise would not have consented to; and (4) the patient was injured by the treatment. It found that the doctor informed the family of the material risks of stenting, including death, and that another physician specializing in stenting would operate. Absent proof that the patient's signature was forged or that he was incapable of giving intelligent consent, the consent forms were valid, and the lack of witnesses' signatures was irrelevant.
suggestedAnswer.application: The doctor explained the alternatives and their risks and disclosed his own limits. Mario's signatures on the forms are not shown to be forged, nor is he shown to have been incapable of consenting. The stroke was an inherent risk that was disclosed and that, per the experts, could not be totally prevented. The parties' own stipulation that stenting has "much less risk" does not mean "risk-free."
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The doctor is not liable. **Bar trap:** a consent form is not void merely because no witness signed it; attack it with proof of forgery or incapacity. And "less risk" is not "risk-free."

keyPoints: Four elements of a lack-of-informed-consent case (restated from Li v. Soliman)
The doctor disclosed the risks, including death, and that a specialist would operate
Signed consent forms are valid absent proof of forgery or incapacity; no witness signatures needed
The stroke was an inherent, disclosed risk of the procedure
"Less risk" is not equivalent to "risk-free"

source.caseTitle: Que v. Philippine Heart Center, et al.
source.part: Ruling, Respondents are not liable for medical negligence (informed consent)
source.excerpt: In a lack of informed consent litigation, the plaintiff must prove the following: (1) the physician had a duty to disclose material risks; (2) the physician failed to disclose or inadequately disclosed those risks; (3) as a direct and proximate result of the failure to disclose, the patient consented to the treatment they otherwise would not have consented to; and (4) the patient was injured by the proposed treatment. … The facts would show that Dr. Aventura informed the Que family, most especially Quintin, of the material risks inherent in the stenting procedure, and that includes death. Dr. Aventura also informed the family that if they decide to continue the operation, another physician will operate on Quintin because he does not specialize in stenting procedures. … To be sure, Quintin signed the Consent for Endovascular Stenting and the Consent to Operation, Administration of Anesthesia, and the Rendering of Other Medical Services. His signature appeared in these documents. On the other hand, Elpidio did not categorically dispute the veracity of Quintin's signature. Absent proof that Quintin's signature was forged or Quintin was incapable of giving intelligent consent when he signed the two documents, we upheld the validity of the consent forms. Accordingly, the lack of signatures of witnesses is irrelevant.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In a suit for the death of a patient after a cardiovascular procedure, the plaintiff's only expert is a forensic pathologist who did the autopsy. The defendant surgeon, whose decades of training and experience in cardiothoracic and vascular surgery are not disputed, presents two cardiovascular surgeons who testify that his advice and treatment were sound. Who should prevail on the issue of negligence? Explain, following Que v. Philippine Heart Center.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The surgeon. The forensic pathologist is not qualified to testify on the standard of care of a cardiovascular surgeon; the surgeon's admitted qualifications raise a presumption that he took the necessary precautions; and the qualified experts support him, so the preponderance of evidence is in his favor.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Que v. Philippine Heart Center, the Court held that the expert witness must be a similarly trained and experienced physician; a forensic pathologist cannot qualify as an expert to determine whether the surgeon exercised the norm observed by other reasonably competent members of the profession. It cited Ramos v. Court of Appeals (a pulmonologist not qualified on the standard of care of an anesthesiologist) and Reyes v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital (an autopsy expert not qualified as a specialist in infectious diseases). It also affirmed the trial court's statement that when the qualifications of a physician are admitted, there is a presumption that in proper cases he takes the necessary precaution and employs the best of his knowledge and skill.
suggestedAnswer.application: The pathologist can speak to the cause of death, but not to what a reasonably competent cardiovascular surgeon would have done. The defense experts, from the same field, testified that the treatment was sound and the complication an inherent risk. With the plaintiff presenting no qualified expert to refute them, and the surgeon's qualifications admitted, the plaintiff cannot prove a breach of the standard of care.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The surgeon prevails; the preponderance of evidence tilts in his favor. **Bar trap:** the person who performed the autopsy is not automatically the right expert on whether the treating doctor met the standard of care.

keyPoints: The expert on the standard of care must be a similarly trained and experienced physician
A forensic pathologist is not qualified to testify on a surgeon's standard of care
Consistent with Ramos (pulmonologist) and Reyes (autopsy expert)
Admitted qualifications raise a presumption that the physician took the necessary precautions
Unrefuted qualified experts tilt the preponderance of evidence

source.caseTitle: Que v. Philippine Heart Center, et al.
source.part: Ruling, expert witnesses and the presumption from qualifications
source.excerpt: Jurisprudence provides that when the qualifications of a physician are admitted, there is a presumption that in proper cases, he takes the necessary precaution and employs the best of his knowledge and skill in attending to his clients. … On the other hand, Elpidio failed to present expert witness to refute Dr. Tuazon's and Dr. Figueroa's statements. As a forensic pathologist, Dr. Fortun cannot qualify as an expert witness in so far as to determine whether Dr. Aventura exercised the norm observed by other reasonably competent members of the profession. The expert witness must be a similarly trained and experienced physician. Thus, we declared in Ramos v. Court of Appeals that a pulmonologist is not qualified to testify as to the standard of care required of an anesthesiologist. In Reyes v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital, we ruled that an autopsy expert is not qualified to testify as a specialist in infectious diseases. Therefore, the preponderance of evidence tilts in favor of respondents.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Distinguish a question of law from a question of fact. In a petition for review on certiorari, the son of a patient who died after a procedure asks the Supreme Court to examine anew whether his father's signatures on the consent forms are genuine and whether the device used was faulty. Are these proper issues? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: A question of law arises when there is doubt as to the applicable law on a certain set of facts and does not call for an examination of the probative value of the evidence; a question of fact arises when there is controversy as to the truth or falsity of the alleged facts. The genuineness of the signatures and the faultiness of the device are questions of fact, beyond review under Rule 45.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Que v. Philippine Heart Center, the Court reiterated that a Rule 45 petition shall raise only questions of law, since the Court is not a trier of facts. The test is not the label the party gives the question, but whether the appellate court can resolve the issue without examining or evaluating the evidence; if the facts are disputed or the issues require an examination of the evidence, the question is one of fact.
suggestedAnswer.application: Deciding whether the father's signatures are genuine, or whether the device was faulty, requires weighing the evidence again (the forms, the testimonies, the expert opinions). These are factual matters already passed upon by the lower courts, so the petition could be dismissed on this basis alone. The Court nonetheless found no reason to disturb the lower courts' findings.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: They are questions of fact, not proper in a Rule 45 petition. **Bar trap:** calling an issue a "question of law" does not make it one; the test is whether it can be resolved without evaluating the evidence.

keyPoints: A Rule 45 petition raises only questions of law; the Court is not a trier of facts
Question of law: doubt as to the applicable law on given facts, without examining the probative value of evidence
Question of fact: controversy as to the truth or falsity of the alleged facts
The test is whether the issue can be resolved without examining or evaluating the evidence, not the label
Genuineness of signatures and faultiness of a device are questions of fact

source.caseTitle: Que v. Philippine Heart Center, et al.
source.part: Ruling, questions of law and of fact under Rule 45
source.excerpt: Prefatorily, we reiterate that a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45 of the Rules of Court shall only raise questions of law. We are not a trier of facts. It is not our function to analyze and weigh the evidence that the lower courts have already passed upon. A question of law arises when there is doubt as to the applicable law and jurisprudence on a certain set of facts. It must not call for an examination of the probative value of the evidence. On the other hand, a question of fact exists when there is controversy as to the truth or falsity of the alleged facts. … The test, therefore, is not the appellation given to a question by the party raising it, but whether the appellate court can resolve the issue without examining or evaluating the evidence, in which case, it is a question of law; otherwise, it is a question of fact. … Elpidio implores the Court to evaluate anew the consent forms signed by his father authorizing the conduct of the stenting procedure as well as the "faultiness" of the stent used during the operation. These are factual matters beyond the Court's power of review under Rule 45. On this basis alone, the Petition should be dismissed.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Que v. Philippine Heart Center, the parties stipulated at pre-trial that stenting, as a "new non-invasive approach," entails "much less risk" than open surgery. The patient's son argued the family understood the procedure to be safe. How was the stipulation read?

choices.A: As an admission by the doctor that the procedure carried no risk at all.
choices.B: As a waiver by the family of any claim for damages.
choices.C: As showing only that stenting carries less risk, which is not equivalent to being risk-free.
choices.D: As proof that the doctor guaranteed the success of the procedure.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court of Appeals, whose ruling the Supreme Court affirmed, noted that one of the stipulated facts was that stenting has been used abroad and entails "much less risk," but "less risk" is not equivalent to being "risk-free." The Supreme Court found that the doctor informed the family of the material risks of stenting, including death. **A and D are wrong:** less risk is neither no risk nor a guarantee. **B is wrong:** the stipulation was not a waiver; the claim failed on the merits. **Bar trap:** a comparison of risks is not a promise of safety.

source.caseTitle: Que v. Philippine Heart Center, et al.
source.part: CA Ruling and Ruling ("less risk" and the stipulation of facts)
source.excerpt: The CA held that there was adequate disclosure of material risks inherent in the stenting procedure. Quintin consented to the procedure, as shown in his signed consent forms. Further, the CA noted that one of the facts stipulated by the parties during the pre-trial conference was that the stenting as the "new non-invasive approach" has been used in the United States and Europe and entails "much less risk." However, "less risk" is not equivalent to being "risk-free."

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A patient suffers a stroke during a stenting procedure, when cholesterol clots dislodged by the catheter travel to the brain; experts testify this is an inherent risk of the procedure. Following Que v. Philippine Heart Center, does res ipsa loquitur apply?

choices.A: No, because the death was due to one of the inherent risks of the procedure, not to the doctor's negligence.
choices.B: Yes, because the patient was unconscious and under the doctors' exclusive control.
choices.C: Yes, because a stroke during a procedure always speaks of negligence.
choices.D: No, because res ipsa loquitur applies only to hospitals, not to doctors.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court listed the elements of res ipsa loquitur (an accident that does not ordinarily occur unless someone is negligent; exclusive control by the person charged; no voluntary action or contribution of the injured person) and held it inapplicable because "[t]he cause of Quintin's death was not due to the negligence of Dr. Aventura but was due to one of the inherent risks of the stenting procedure." **B is wrong:** exclusive control is not enough when the first element (an occurrence that does not ordinarily happen without negligence) is missing. **C is wrong:** an inherent risk can materialize even with proper care. **D is wrong:** the doctrine is not so limited. **Bar trap:** a known, inherent risk is the opposite of an occurrence that "speaks for itself" of negligence.

source.caseTitle: Que v. Philippine Heart Center, et al.
source.part: Ruling, res ipsa loquitur
source.excerpt: Moreover, the doctrine of res ipsa loquitor, translated as "the thing speaks for itself," does not apply in this case. The doctrine requires the concurrence of the following elements: (1) the accident was of a kind that does not ordinarily occur unless someone is negligent; (2) the instrumentality or agency which caused the injury was under the exclusive control of the person charged with negligence; and (3) the injury suffered must not have been due to any voluntary action or contribution from the injured person. The cause of Quintin's death was not due to the negligence of Dr. Aventura but was due to one of the inherent risks of the stenting procedure.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Why did the Court in Que v. Philippine Heart Center hold that negligence was not the proximate cause of the patient's death?

choices.A: Because the patient's son failed to pay the hospital bill.
choices.B: Because a foreign doctor performed the procedure, which breaks the chain of causation.
choices.C: Because the autopsy was done by a private pathologist.
choices.D: Because, according to the experts, the stroke was an inherent risk of stenting and would have occurred even if the stent had been successfully deployed.

questions.explanation: **D is correct.** After defining proximate cause as that which, in a natural and continuous sequence, unbroken by any efficient intervening cause, produces injury, the Court relied on the experts: the stroke "was one of the inherent risks involved in a stenting procedure," and "Quintin would have had a stroke regardless of whether the device was successfully deployed on him or not." **A and C are wrong:** neither was a basis of the ruling. **B is wrong:** the Court upheld the foreign specialist's authority to operate under the PHC's charter; his participation did not, by itself, break causation. **Bar trap:** if the same harm would have occurred even with a successful procedure, the alleged failure is not the proximate cause.

source.caseTitle: Que v. Philippine Heart Center, et al.
source.part: Ruling, proximate cause
source.excerpt: Negligence was not the proximate cause of Quintin's death. Proximate cause is that which, in a natural and continuous sequence, unbroken by any efficient intervening cause, produces injury, without which the result would not have occurred. … The expert witnesses, Dr. Tuazon and Dr. Figueroa, testified that the stroke experienced by Quintin, which led to his death, was one of the inherent risks involved in a stenting procedure. To be sure, Quintin would have had a stroke regardless of whether the device was successfully deployed on him or not.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: The patient's son in Que v. Philippine Heart Center pointed out that the foreign specialist who performed the procedure was not admitted to practice medicine in the Philippines. What allowed the Philippine Heart Center to have him operate?

choices.A: The patient's signed consent alone, which cures any lack of license.
choices.B: Section 5 of Presidential Decree No. 673 (the PHC's charter), which allows it to invite foreign heart specialists and similar experts to train its personnel, trainees or residents, and a certification listing him as one of the experts who operated there.
choices.C: The general rule that any foreign doctor may practice in a government hospital.
choices.D: The distributor's contract with the manufacturer of the stent.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court noted that under Section 5 of Presidential Decree No. 673, the PHC may "invite foreign heart specialists and similar experts in the various medical fields to train the personnel or trainees or residents of the [PHC]," and that a former PHC director certified that the specialist was one of the experts who operated in the PHC. **A is wrong:** the ruling on his authority rested on the charter, not on consent. **C is wrong:** the Court relied on the PHC's specific charter provision, not on any general rule. **D is wrong:** the distribution contract had nothing to do with the authority to operate. **Bar trap:** look for the specific legal authority for a foreign specialist's participation.

source.caseTitle: Que v. Philippine Heart Center, et al.
source.part: Ruling, the foreign specialist's authority to operate
source.excerpt: As to Dr. Verhoeven' s authority to operate on Quintin, Section 5 of Presidential Decree No. 673, the PHC allows the hospital to "invite foreign heart specialists and similar experts in the various medical fields to train the personnel or trainees or residents of the [PHC]." Dr. Ludgerio D. Torres, former director of the PHC, issued a Certification dated January 25, 2013, listing Dr. Verhoeven as one of the experts in his field to have operated in the PHC.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: The patient's son in Que v. Philippine Heart Center claimed that a faulty stent hastened his father's death, relying on the foreign specialist's remark after the procedure that the device was "faulty" and on his and his sister's testimony. How did the Court rule?

choices.A: It held the distributor liable, because any device that fails during surgery is presumed defective.
choices.B: It remanded the case to determine the defect.
choices.C: It rejected the claim: bare allegations are not proof, and the records did not show how the stent was faulty.
choices.D: It held the hospital liable as the user of the device.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court said it "cannot subscribe to Elpidio's claim that the 'faulty' stent hastened the death of his father. Bare allegations are not proof," noting that apart from the testimonies of the son and his sister, the records did not show how the stent was faulty. The experts also testified that the stroke would have occurred even if the stent had been deployed. **A is wrong:** no such presumption was applied; the claimant must prove the defect. **B is wrong:** no remand was ordered. **D is wrong:** the hospital was not held liable. **Bar trap:** a remark that a device was "faulty," without more, does not prove a defect.

source.caseTitle: Que v. Philippine Heart Center, et al.
source.part: Ruling, the claim of a faulty stent
source.excerpt: Finally, we cannot subscribe to Elpidio's claim that the "faulty" stent hastened the death of his father. Bare allegations are not proof. The trial court noted that other than the testimonies of Elpidio and his sister, Elisa Que, the records do not show how faulty the stent used on Quintin was.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: How is a physician-patient relationship created? Does a second-year hospital resident who, while doing rounds, examines a patient assigned to another doctor and prescribes a course of treatment, owe that patient a duty of care? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: A physician-patient relationship is created when a patient engages the services of a physician and the physician accepts or agrees to provide care. It is consensual, but the consent need not be express; it may be implied from the physician's affirmative action to diagnose or treat the patient, or participation in it. The resident therefore owes the patient a duty of care.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Casumpang v. Cortejo, the Court held that duty requires proof of a professional relationship between physician and patient; without it, a physician owes no duty and incurs no liability. The mere fact that a person approaches a physician and seeks advice or treatment does not create the duty unless the physician agrees. Once the relationship is established, the physician must use at least the standard of care of a reasonably competent doctor under similar circumstances. A resident tasked to do rounds and assist other physicians is deemed to have agreed to the relationship when she participates in the diagnosis and prescribes treatment (citing Jarcia v. People and foreign cases on residents' supervision).
suggestedAnswer.application: By examining the patient and prescribing a course of treatment, the resident performed affirmative acts of diagnosis and treatment, which amount to acceptance of the relationship and the duty of care that comes with it, even though the patient was assigned to another doctor.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Yes, the resident owes a duty of care. **Bar trap:** a request for help alone does not create the relationship, but once the doctor examines or treats, acceptance is implied; whether the resident is liable then depends on whether she breached the standard (in Casumpang, the resident was ultimately not liable).

keyPoints: Duty requires a physician-patient relationship
Created when the patient engages the physician and the physician accepts; it is consensual
Consent may be implied from affirmative acts of diagnosis or treatment
Merely approaching a physician does not create the duty unless the physician agrees
A resident who participates in diagnosis and prescribes treatment accepts the relationship

source.caseTitle: Casumpang, et al. v. Cortejo
source.part: Our Ruling, The Elements of a Medical Malpractice Suit (the physician-patient relationship)
source.excerpt: Duty refers to the standard of behavior that imposes restrictions on one's conduct. It requires proof of professional relationship between the physician and the patient. Without the professional relationship, a physician owes no duty to the patient, and cannot therefore incur any liability. A physician-patient relationship is created when a patient engages the services of a physician, and the latter accepts or agrees to provide care to the patient. The establishment of this relationship is consensual, and the acceptance by the physician essential. The mere fact that an individual approaches a physician and seeks diagnosis, advice or treatment does not create the duty of care unless the physician agrees. The consent needed to create the relationship does not always need to be express. In the absence of an express agreement, a physician-patient relationship may be implied from the physician’s affirmative action to diagnose and/or treat a patient, or in his participation in such diagnosis and/or treatment. … With respect to Dr. Sanga, her professional relationship with Edmer arose when she assumed the obligation to provide resident supervision over the latter. As second year resident doctor tasked to do rounds and assist other physicians, Dr. Sanga is deemed to have agreed to the creation of physician-patient relationship with the hospital’s patients when she participated in the diagnosis and prescribed a course of treatment for Edmer.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A pediatrician diagnosed a feverish boy with bronchopneumonia using only a stethoscope and a chest X-ray, and kept to that diagnosis although the mother told him the boy had high fever but no cough, chest and stomach pain, and blood in his sputum. He ordered blood tests only after the boy's third episode of bleeding; the tests showed dengue hemorrhagic fever, and the boy died. The pediatrician argues that a wrong diagnosis is not malpractice, since medicine is not an exact science. Is he liable? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. A wrong diagnosis is not by itself malpractice, but it becomes evidence of malpractice when it results from negligent conduct, such as failing to recognize symptoms and to order the appropriate tests, as here.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Casumpang v. Cortejo, the Court held that it does not decide the correctness of a doctor's diagnosis but whether a breach of duty took place; that physicians are generally not liable for damages resulting from a bona fide error of judgment; and that medicine is not an exact science, so even specialists are not expected to be 100% accurate. But when the erroneous diagnosis was the result of negligent conduct (neglect of medical history, failure to order the appropriate tests, failure to recognize symptoms), it becomes evidence of medical malpractice; the doctor must act according to acceptable medical practice standards.
suggestedAnswer.application: The boy's rapid breathing, chest and stomach pain, fever and blood in the saliva were, per the expert, classic signs of dengue. The pediatrician selectively appreciated only the symptoms that fit bronchopneumonia, ignored the information that pointed to dengue, did not examine the source of the bleeding, and ordered confirmatory tests too late. That is negligence in the diagnosis, followed by delayed management of the disease, which caused the death since dengue, timely diagnosed and managed, is not usually fatal.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The pediatrician is liable. **Bar trap:** "an honest error of judgment" protects only a diagnosis reached with due care; a wrong diagnosis reached by ignoring symptoms and skipping tests is negligence.

keyPoints: A wrong diagnosis is not by itself malpractice; bona fide errors of judgment are generally not actionable
Medicine is not an exact science; 100% accuracy is not expected
An erroneous diagnosis resulting from negligent conduct (neglected history, no appropriate tests, unrecognized symptoms) is evidence of malpractice
The doctor selectively appreciated symptoms and ordered tests too late
Timely diagnosis and management would have substantially reduced the risk of death

source.caseTitle: Casumpang, et al. v. Cortejo
source.part: Our Ruling, Dr. Casumpang's Negligence (negligence in the diagnosis)
source.excerpt: First, we emphasize that we do not decide the correctness of a doctor’s diagnosis, or the accuracy of the medical findings and treatment. Our duty in medical malpractice cases is to decide – based on the evidence adduced and expert opinion presented– whether a breach of duty took place. Second, we clarify that a wrong diagnosis is not by itself medical malpractice. Physicians are generally not liable for damages resulting from a bona fide error of judgment. Nonetheless, when the physician’s erroneous diagnosis was the result of negligent conduct (e.g., neglect of medical history, failure to order the appropriate tests, failure to recognize symptoms), it becomes an evidence of medical malpractice. Third, we also note that medicine is not an exact science; and doctors, or even specialists, are not expected to give a 100% accurate diagnosis in treating patients who come to their clinic for consultations. Error is possible as the exercise of judgment is called for in considering and reading the exhibited symptoms, the results of tests, and in arriving at definitive conclusions. But in doing all these, the doctor must have acted according to acceptable medical practice standards. In the present case, evidence on record established that in confirming the diagnosis of bronchopneumonia, Dr. Casumpang selectively appreciated some and not all of the symptoms presented, and failed to promptly conduct the appropriate tests to confirm his findings. In sum, Dr. Casumpang failed to timely detect dengue fever, which failure, especially when reasonable prudence would have shown that indications of dengue were evident and/or foreseeable, constitutes negligence.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Parents with no doctor of their own brought their sick son to a hospital's emergency room on their family doctor's referral to the hospital. Using their health-plan card, they were assigned by the hospital to a pediatrician accredited with the plan; no one told them he was an independent contractor. The son died through the pediatrician's negligence. The hospital argues that the pediatrician is not its employee, since it does not control his diagnosis and treatment, and that the parents chose him through their health plan. Is the hospital liable? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. Although there is no employer-employee relationship for lack of control, the hospital is solidarily liable under the doctrine of apparent authority, and the use of the health plan does not change this.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Casumpang v. Cortejo, the Court held that control, the most crucial element of an employer-employee relationship, was absent, so the doctors were independent contractors and Article 2180 did not apply. As a rule hospitals are not liable for the negligence of independent contractors, but they are liable if the physician acts as the hospital's ostensible agent. Following Nogales v. Capitol Medical Center, the plaintiff must prove two factors: the hospital's manifestations (which may be general and implied) and the patient's reliance on the hospital rather than on a specific physician, consistent with ordinary care and prudence. The use of a health care plan only limits the choice of physicians to those accredited with it, not the liability of the doctors or the hospital.
suggestedAnswer.application: The parents knew no doctor at the hospital and came because of a referral to the hospital itself; the hospital assigned the pediatrician and never told them he was an independent contractor, thereby holding him out as part of its staff. The parents relied on the hospital to provide care, not on a doctor of their own choosing, and did not know, nor should have known, that he was an independent contractor. Estoppel has set in.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The hospital is solidarily liable with the pediatrician under apparent authority. **Bar trap:** absence of control defeats only Article 2180; and a health-plan card limits choice, not liability.

keyPoints: No employer-employee relationship: control, the most crucial element, was absent
Hospitals are generally not liable for independent contractors, except under apparent authority
Two factors: the hospital's manifestations (may be implied) and the patient's reliance on the hospital
The hospital assigned the doctor without disclosing his status; the parents relied on the hospital
A health-care plan limits the choice of doctors, not liability

source.caseTitle: Casumpang, et al. v. Cortejo
source.part: Our Ruling, Liability of SJDH
source.excerpt: Control, which is the most crucial among the elements, is not present in this case. Based on the records, no evidence exists showing that SJDH exercised any degree of control over the means, methods of procedure and manner by which the petitioning doctors conducted and performed their medical profession. … As a rule, hospitals are not liable for the negligence of its independent contractors. However, it may be found liable if the physician or independent contractor acts as an ostensible agent of the hospital. This exception is also known as the "doctrine of apparent authority." … In sum, a hospital can be held vicariously liable for the negligent acts of a physician (or an independent contractor) providing care at the hospital if the plaintiff can prove these two factors: first, the hospital’s manifestations; and second, the patient’s reliance. … Based on the records, the respondent relied on SJDH rather than upon Dr. Casumpang, to care and treat his son Edmer. His testimony during trial showed that he and his wife did not know any doctors at SJDH; they also did not know that Dr. Casumpang was an independent contractor. They brought their son to SJDH for diagnosis because of their family doctor’s referral. … We also stress that Mrs. Cortejo’s use of health care plan (Fortune Care) did not affect SJDH’s liability. The only effect of the availment of her Fortune Care card benefits is that her choice of physician is limited only to physicians who are accredited with Fortune Care. Thus, her use of health care plan in this case only limited the choice of doctors (or coverage of services, amount etc.) and not the liability of doctors or the hospital.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Casumpang v. Cortejo, why was the resident physician, Dr. Sanga, not held liable even though she, like the attending physician, assumed that the blood in the patient's phlegm came from bronchopneumonia?

choices.A: Because residents are held to a lower standard of care than licensed physicians.
choices.B: Because her error was an honest mistake of judgment, given the diagnosis already made by two doctors, the attending physician's burden of final diagnosis, and her diligent care once she suspected dengue.
choices.C: Because residents owe no duty of care to patients assigned to an attending physician.
choices.D: Because she was an employee of the hospital, which alone answers for her.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court found Dr. Sanga "not entirely faultless," but considering the diagnosis previously made by two doctors and that "the burden of final diagnosis pertains to the attending physician," her error "was merely an honest mistake of judgment influenced in no small measure by her status in the hospital hierarchy." She also ran tests and notified the attending physician once she suspected dengue. **A is wrong:** the Court said residents are subject to the same standard of care as physicians generally, though liability considers authority and supervision. **C is wrong:** she had a physician-patient relationship and a duty of care. **D is wrong:** the Court found no employer-employee relationship with the hospital as to the petitioning doctors. **Bar trap:** residents have no immunity, but the attending physician bears the principal responsibility.

source.caseTitle: Casumpang, et al. v. Cortejo
source.part: Our Ruling, Dr. Sanga is Not Liable for Negligence
source.excerpt: Based on her statements we find that Dr. Sanga was not entirely faultless. Nevertheless, her failure to discern the import of Edmer’s second bleeding does not necessarily amount to negligence as the respondent himself admitted that Dr. Sanga failed to examine the blood specimen because he wash edit away. In addition, considering the diagnosis previously made by two doctors, and the uncontroverted fact that the burden of final diagnosis pertains to the attending physician (in this case, Dr. Casumpang), we believe that Dr. Sanga’s error was merely an honest mistake of judgment influenced in no small measure by her status in the hospital hierarchy; hence, she should not be held liable for medical negligence.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Casumpang v. Cortejo, the doctors objected that the plaintiff's expert on dengue was a pathologist, not a pediatrician. How did the Court rule?

choices.A: The pathologist was disqualified, because an expert's specialty must always match the defendant's.
choices.B: The pathologist was disqualified, following Ramos v. Court of Appeals.
choices.C: The pathologist was qualified, because what governs is the witness's knowledge of and familiarity with the standard of care, not the classification by title or specialty; he had relevant exposure in pediatrics and had handled many dengue cases.
choices.D: Expert testimony was unnecessary, because res ipsa loquitur applied.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court held that in Ramos and Cereno the experts were disqualified mainly for their incapacity to shed light on the standard of care; a mismatch of specialties is "at most, one of the considerations." It is "the scope of the witness' knowledge and not the artificial classification by title" that governs. Dr. Jaudian had attended at least 30 Pediatric Society seminars, practiced for 16 years and handled at least 50 dengue cases, showing sufficient familiarity with the standard of care. **A and B are wrong** for the same reason. **D is wrong:** the Court relied on expert testimony; res ipsa loquitur was not the basis. **Bar trap:** compare Que v. Philippine Heart Center (2025), where a forensic pathologist was not qualified on a cardiovascular surgeon's standard of care; the test is familiarity with the specific standard, not the title.

source.caseTitle: Casumpang, et al. v. Cortejo
source.part: Our Ruling, Dr. Jaudian's Professional Competence and Credibility
source.excerpt: A close scrutiny of Ramos and Cereno reveals that the Court primarily based the witnesses’ disqualification to testify as an expert on their incapacity to shed light on the standard of care that must be observed by the defendant-physicians. That the expert witnesses’ specialties do not match the physicians’ practice area only constituted, at most, one of the considerations that should not be taken out of context. After all, the sole function of a medical expert witness, regardless of his/her specialty, is to afford assistance to the courts on medical matters, and to explain the medical facts in issue. … Although he specializes in pathology, it was established during trial that he had attended not less than 30 seminars held by the Pediatric Society, had exposure in pediatrics, had been practicing medicine for 16 years, and had handled not less than 50 dengue related cases. As a licensed medical practitioner specializing in pathology, who had practical and relevant exposure in pediatrics and dengue related cases, we are convinced that Dr. Jaudian demonstrated sufficient familiarity with the standard of care to be applied in dengue fever cases.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: According to the guideline cited in Casumpang v. Cortejo (from Evans v. Ohanesian), what must be shown to qualify a witness as a medical expert?

choices.A: That the witness is a board-certified specialist in the same field as the defendant.
choices.B: That the witness has examined the patient personally.
choices.C: That the witness is employed by a government hospital.
choices.D: That the witness (1) has the required professional knowledge, learning and skill of the subject under inquiry sufficient to speak with authority on it, and (2) is familiar with the standard required of a physician under similar circumstances.

questions.explanation: **D is correct.** The Court quoted Evans v. Ohanesian: the witness must "(1) [have] the required professional knowledge, learning and skill of the subject under inquiry sufficient to qualify him to speak with authority on the subject; and (2) [be] familiar with the standard required of a physician under similar circumstances"; the degree of his knowledge then goes to the weight rather than the admissibility of his opinion. **A is wrong:** the Court said it is not critical whether the expert is a general practitioner or a specialist, so long as he exhibits knowledge of the subject. **B and C are wrong:** neither is a requirement. **Bar trap:** specialty and training go to weight, not admissibility.

source.caseTitle: Casumpang, et al. v. Cortejo
source.part: Our Ruling, Criteria in Qualifying as an Expert Witness (citing Evans v. Ohanesian)
source.excerpt: To qualify a witness as a medical expert, it must be shown that the witness (1) has the required professional knowledge, learning and skill of the subject under inquiry sufficient to qualify him to speak with authority on the subject; and (2) is familiar with the standard required of a physician under similar circumstances; where a witness has disclosed sufficient knowledge of the subject to entitle his opinion to go to the jury, the question of the degree of his knowledge goes more to the weight of the evidence than to its admissibility.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Casumpang v. Cortejo, the patient's mother used her health-care plan card, so she was limited to doctors accredited with the plan. What effect did this have on the hospital's liability?

choices.A: None: the plan only limited her choice of doctors (or the coverage of services), not the liability of the doctors or the hospital.
choices.B: It made the health-care plan company solely liable.
choices.C: It freed the hospital, since the mother chose the doctor through her plan.
choices.D: It made the hospital liable under Article 2180 as the doctor's employer.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court said the mother's use of her health-care plan "did not affect SJDH's liability. The only effect of the availment of her Fortune Care card benefits is that her choice of physician is limited only to physicians who are accredited with Fortune Care. Thus, her use of health care plan in this case only limited the choice of doctors (or coverage of services, amount etc.) and not the liability of doctors or the hospital." **B is wrong:** the plan company's liability was not in issue. **C is wrong:** the hospital itself assigned the doctor and held him out. **D is wrong:** the Court found no employer-employee relationship; liability rested on apparent authority. **Bar trap:** a health plan is not a defense to apparent authority.

source.caseTitle: Casumpang, et al. v. Cortejo
source.part: Our Ruling, SJDH Clothed Dr. Casumpang With Apparent Authority (the health-care plan)
source.excerpt: We also stress that Mrs. Cortejo’s use of health care plan (Fortune Care) did not affect SJDH’s liability. The only effect of the availment of her Fortune Care card benefits is that her choice of physician is limited only to physicians who are accredited with Fortune Care. Thus, her use of health care plan in this case only limited the choice of doctors (or coverage of services, amount etc.) and not the liability of doctors or the hospital.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Among the four elements of an employer-employee relationship, which did Casumpang v. Cortejo describe as "the most crucial"?

choices.A: Selection and engagement of services.
choices.B: Payment of wages.
choices.C: Control, that is, the power to control not only the end to be achieved but the means to be used in reaching it.
choices.D: The power to hire and fire.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** After listing the four elements (selection and engagement; payment of wages; the power to hire and fire; and the power to control the end and the means), the Court said: "Control, which is the most crucial among the elements, is not present in this case," since the hospital did not control the doctors' diagnosis and treatment or supervise their handling of the case. **A, B and D are wrong:** they are elements, but not the one singled out. **Bar trap:** without control, a hospital is not liable under Article 2180, but it may still be liable under apparent authority.

source.caseTitle: Casumpang, et al. v. Cortejo
source.part: Our Ruling, There is No Employer-Employee Relationship Between SJDH and the Petitioning Doctors
source.excerpt: In determining whether an employer-employee relationship exists between the parties, the following elements must be present: (1) selection and engagement of services; (2) payment of wages; (3) the power to hire and fire; and (4) the power to control not only the end to be achieved, but the means to be used in reaching such an end. Control, which is the most crucial among the elements, is not present in this case.
